en: The Compendium of Dhāraṇīs — (1) @ — (2) @ — (3) Oṃ! Homage to the glorious Vajrasattva.
In the speech of Vajrasattva: Blue, blue, blue in form; empty, empty, great emptiness; blue expanse, blue in form; from the ocean of immortals, there is no earth. || 1 ||
The body of the Manava sage, having entered the womb of the fish within the circle of the Matsya kingdom, was protected from falling into the midst of heaven by the application of unguents. || 2 ||
O Goddess, take hold of the mind; O Vajrasattva, [take hold of] the auspicious Prajñāpāramitā-vajra; O Vajra, [take hold of] the bell, the Prajñāpāramitā. || 3 ||

Born from the eyes of Vairocana, he is the one born from the head; in the left sacrificial pit, he is the one with intense radiance and unshakeable vision, bearing a banner, a vajra, and a bell, with a jewel at his navel and an unfailing hand.
Amitābha arises from the jewel-eye on the forehead as the western face; Amoghasiddhi is on the left. || 5 ||
May I become four-faced, possessing the great luster of Vairocana, with white, dark-brown, and very brilliant [complexions], and white, yellow, black, and red [eyes]. 6.
The supreme Guru Vajrācārya, the auspicious bearer of the vajra-bell.
Anointed with wisdom and primordial gnosis, he is the source of all Tathāgatas. || 7 ||

O Lord of the World, you who have arisen from the rays [of light], who are the multitude of those who traverse the sky, who are the source of the two ears of the donkey of action, and who are the life-force of the hand-born [Arjuna]—[I bow to you].
From the destruction of the mire of all mental afflictions and obscurations, there arises this compassion, which is the seed of Samantabhadra. || 9 ||

On the middle of the right arm is Amama; on the right shoulder is Andhāntamara; on the right side of the waist is Pātālasaṃskṛta; on the face of the left arm is Āntaka; on the neck is Aparājita; and on the left side of the waist is Amitakṣuṇuli. || 10 ||
The great lord, whose arms were like venomous serpents, who was adorned with saffron and blue lotuses, and who possessed the splendor of a swan. || 11 ||
I am she who dwells within the bodies of the intermediate space between the Uṣṇīṣa-cakravartin and the heavens, and who is adorned by the netherworlds of Andha, Antaka, Hararāja, and Pātāla. 12.
Then, from the perfection of wisdom, there arose the sphere of clouds in the sky, possessing the luster of a grove of *rāma-keśa* flowers produced by the assembly of the four gods. 13.
May the goddess Māharatisagadveṣarati, who is radiant with passion for me, grant me delight free from old age. || 14 ||
The earth, fire, wind, water, ether, the sun, the moon, the stars, and the planets—these are proclaimed as the eight Tārās. (15)
The words of Vajrasattva:
Establishing the four directions with the youth of the universal vajra, the pure vajra dwells in the midst of the sky-like expanse of space; to that which is unshakeable, homage! 16.
In that regard, Vairocana is in the east, Ratnasambhava in the south, Amitābha in the west, and Amoghasiddhi is said to be in the north. || 17 ||
In the south-east corner is Saṃrocanā; in the south-west is the goddess Māmekī; in the north-west is the goddess Purādevī; and in the north-east is the goddess Oṃkārā. || 18 ||

Thus, O Agni, the eastern direction has arrows as its weapon; the south-western has horses as its weapon; the north-western has fragrances as its weapon; and the lord of the north-east has tastes as its weapon.
To the east, to the image of Vākya, [offer] Maitrī; to the south, to the image of Kṣiti, [offer] Vajrapāṇi, who has gone to heaven. || 20 ||
In the fifth position from the eastern direction are Lokeśvararāja, Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin, Samantabhadra, and Uttara. (21)
Yamāntaka is at the eastern gate, Prajñāntaka at the southern gate, Padmāntaka at the western gate, and Vighnāntaka at the northern gate. (22)
In the northeast corner is Acara, and in the southeast corner is Tārkīrāja.
(6) Neṛtroska, Nīladaṇu, Vāyūvāsya, and Mahāvana. || 23 ||
May the Tathāgata, who pervades the cardinal and intermediate directions, become for existence as the earth is for the lotus, and may he become the diamond armor.
Thus ends the hundred [stanzas] on the Tathāgata pervading the body of Śrī Vajrasattva.
May it be auspicious.
The phrase beginning with "the dharmas," etc.
Oṃ, homage to the Buddha; homage to the Guru, homage to the Dharma.
Homage to the Sangha of protectors.
Homage to the Great-Souled One!

Those gods who dwell on Mount Meru, those in the excellent Kanakamālā and Maṇḍūka, those in the Pātāla underworld, and those in Jaṅgāskaṇi, whose rays of light from their jewels have dispelled all darkness above; [to them I bow].

On Mount Kailāsa, amidst the splendors of the gods, all the lords of the Vidyādharas, Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Nāgas—whose hearts were filled with joy—arrived, desiring to hear the words of the supreme sage, which serve as the gateway to liberation; they came all together, eager to listen to that speech which reveals the way to the Asuras.

Kumbhāṇḍas, Kinnara-lords, Garuḍas, Hari, Hara, Śakra, Vṛṣa, and other gods—having offered worship with the five services, they bowed their heads in salutation. That which is difficult to obtain, which I recite through devotion, having bowed down with my head—that Great Sacrifice Sūtra:
Homage to the Buddha, homage to the Dharma, homage to the Saṅgha. (7)
Oṃ, homage to Mañjunātha!
Then there was the illustrious Vajradhana, the supreme tamer of the difficult-to-tame.
The hero who conquers the three worlds, the Lord of the Guhyakas, the master of the Kuliśa. || 1 ||
The lotus-faced one, whose face is like a blossomed white lotus, has his arms extended.
Wisdom is the cave, the supreme vajra, one's own leader, again and again. || 2 ||
Bowing down before the Lord of the Gods, whose abundant waves of frowns are like thunderbolts.
Repeatedly with noble taming methods, and repeatedly with forms that are loathsome.
3. Concealing his own hands with millions of lotuses.
Skillful means and great compassion are supreme for those who act for the benefit of the world. || 4 ||

He saw the Lord together with those who had performed the deeds of a Buddha, whose bodies were formidable and fierce, yet who were intent on blessing beings, and whose forms were bowed in prostration.
Having prostrated to the Lord, the Fully Awakened One, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata.
And having become a great lion, he stood right there before him. || 6 ||
O Lord, do not abandon me to my misfortune; out of compassion for me, O All-pervading One, grant that I may attain perfect enlightenment through the Net of Illusion. (7)

This is not the time for the abandonment of those who are foremost in merit, who are emaciated and distressed like reeds; for the sake of all sentient beings, one must not be resentful when the fruit has perished. (8)
May the Blessed One, the Teacher, the Guru of the World, reveal it.
At the great assembly, he was a knower of reality, one who had transcended the latent tendencies of the senses.
The knowledge of the Blessed One is the very embodiment of the knowledge of the Self-existent Being. || 10 ||
Profound in meaning, noble in meaning, great in meaning, impartial, and auspicious.
The supreme compendium of names, which bestows the fruit at the beginning, middle, and end. || 11 ||
He who has been spoken of by those Buddhas who have passed away will be terrified by those yet to come.
And that which is spoken again and again by the perfectly awakened ones of the present. || 12 ||
In the great tantra *Māyājāla*, as many [deities] as are proclaimed therein—
The Great Vajra was held, gazed upon, and delighted by those who uphold the mantras. || 13 ||
And I, firm in my resolve, shall uphold this and provide for its preservation.
Just as I am, O Lord, the holder of the secrets of all the perfectly awakened ones.
I shall reveal [it] for the sake of sentient beings, according to the particularity of their inclinations.
For the complete destruction of all emaciation and for the total removal of all ignorance. || 15 ||
Thus, having spoken with such boldness, Guhyadru addressed the Tathāgata.
Having joined his palms in reverence, he stood before him with folded wings.
(9) The sixteenth chapter: Verses on Knowledge for Bestowing Blessings. || 0 ||
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Buddha, the supreme among bipeds, withdrew that auspicious tongue from his own mouth.
He who displays a smile to the world is named the Purifier of the Three Lower Realms.
The weapon that illuminates the three worlds, the sword that slays the four Māras.
Then, filling the three worlds with her voice, sweet as honey, she spoke.
He addressed the mighty Lord of the Guhyakas, who holds a thunderbolt in his hand.
To the glorious one who possesses the wealth of the true vajra, who holds the true thunderbolt in his hand—
He who possesses the intellect that perceives all beings as his own self, and who is endowed with great compassion, is a cow. || 4 ||
Having heard this pure Saṃgīti, which contains the ultimate great meaning and destroys poverty, [one attains the goal].
Therefore, [the assembly] has gathered to hear from Mañjuśrī, who abides in the body of the mind. || 5 ||
Therefore, O Lord of the Gods, I shall explain this to you; listen with a one-pointed mind, for he is the Blessed One.
The sixfold reply.
Then the Blessed One, the Sage Aśoka, taught the great [tantra] of the entire family of mantras.
Behold the family of mantra-vidyādharas and the three families!
Lokāloka is the Bhurakula family; Lokāloka-kula is the Mahat family.
The family of Mahāmudrā has been revealed, as well as the great family of Mahoṣṇīṣa. || 2 ||
Two verses on the observation of the six families. || 2 ||
The Lord of Speech then spoke these verses, which are endowed with these six kings of mantras, which arise from non-duality, and whose nature is non-arising.
a ā i ī u ū e ai o au aṃ aḥ ||
Abiding in the heart.
I am the embodiment of wisdom, the Buddha of all Buddhas belonging to the three times.
Oṃ Vajratīkṣṇa, you who sever suffering, embodiment of wisdom and primordial knowledge!
Homage to Jñānakāyavāgīśvara, the Lord Arapacana. || 3 ||
Three verses on the stages of awakening through the Net of Illusion. 3.
Just as the Blessed Buddha is the Fully Awakened One, born from the syllable A.
The syllable A is the foremost of all phonemes, the great meaning, the supreme syllable. || 1 ||
The Great Breath is non-arising, free from the intake of food.
The supreme cause of all verbal expression, he is the illuminator of all speech. || 2 ||
The great festival, the great passion, who brings delight to all sentient beings.
The great, great, and most powerful hatred, the great enemy of all afflictions. || 3 ||
(11) He who destroys the efforts of the intellect, hidden within the great, great delusion.
The great festival, the great wrathful one, the great enemy of wrath, the Great One.
The great festival, the great removal [of defilements], the destroyer of all greed.
He is great passion, great bliss, and the delight that plunges into great delusion. || 5 ||
He has a great form, a great body, a great complexion, and a great physique.
He is of great name, most generous, and possesses a vast and expansive mandala.
He who possesses the great wisdom that upholds the Dharma, and who is the foremost leader for those distressed by great afflictions.
He is of great renown, of great fame, of great light, and of great splendor.
The wise one who possesses the great illusion, the accomplisher of the purpose of the great illusion.
O Mahāmāyā, delighting in the forest of illusion, O Mahāmāyā, you who possess a garland of rays! || 8 ||
The supreme great lord of offerings, the foremost leader who upholds the great ethical discipline.
The steadfast one who possesses great strides, the great hero of noble prowess. || 9 ||
Established in the meditative absorptions of great dhyāna, he bears the body of great wisdom.
Possessing great strength and great skillful means, he is an ocean of the knowledge of his vows. || 10 ||
I am Mahāmaitrī, I am Mahākāruṇika, and I am Ugradhī.
Possessing great wisdom, great intelligence, great skillful means, and great form. || 11 ||
Possessing the power of great supernormal faculties, possessing great speed, and possessing great... (12) velocity.
He possesses two great tusks, has large temples, and is endowed with great strength and prowess.
The shatterer of the great mountain of existence, the wielder of the great vajra, the one who bestows wealth. || 14 ||
Extremely cruel, extremely fierce, the great terror, the inspirer of fear. || 13 ||
The great lord who dispels the darkness [of ignorance], the supreme master of great mantras.
He is established in the method of the Mahāyāna; he is the supreme method of the Mahāyāna. || 14 ||
The Great Mañjuśrī Gāthā on the Vajra Realm, the fourteenth. || 14 ||
Buddha Mahāvairocana is the great observer of silence, the great sage.
The method of the Great Mantra is invoked; it is the Great Mantra, whose very nature is that [mantra]. || 1 ||
He has attained the ten perfections and is one who hears the ten perfections.
The purity of the ten perfections is the method of the ten perfections. || 2 ||
The Lord, the Sovereign of the Ten Stages, is established upon the ten stages.
He whose self is purified by the ten knowledges, who upholds the purification of the ten [faculties]. || 3 ||
The Lord of Sages, who possesses ten forms, who seeks the ten goals, who is endowed with the ten powers, and who is the Knower.
He who accomplishes the welfare of the entire universe, the great lord who masters the ten aspects.
He is beginningless, of a nature free from conceptual proliferation, the pure self, and whose essence is suchness.
He is the Upholder, the Compiler, the speaker of reality, the speaker of truth, the one who acts according to his word, and whose speech is never otherwise. (13, 5)
Non-dual yet speaking of duality, established at the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), he is the lion’s roar of selflessness that strikes terror into the deer-like followers of false paths.
His movement is everywhere unerring and has come thus; he is as swift as thought, the Conqueror, the victor over enemies, the triumphant universal monarch of great power. || 7 ||
In the leader of the host, he is the teacher of the host, the lord of the host, and the master of the host.
Of great majesty, the son of Dhṛtī, he who cannot be led by others, the one of great conduct. || 8 ||
Lord of Speech, Master of Words, eloquent, the one who causes speech to flow, the one of infinite song, truthful in speech, a speaker of truth, the protector, and the teacher of truth. || 9 ||
He is one who does not return to this world, a non-returner, a space-goer, a solitary leader, one who has emerged through various paths of departure, and the sole cause of the great elements.
A monk who has conquered his senses, who is free from passion, who has attained tranquility and reached fearlessness, is called one who is pure and undisturbed by the elements. 11.

Endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, who has transcended the world, is free from defilement and free from egoism; established in the two truths, he stands at the further shore of saṃsāra. Like a ferryman standing on dry land, he is one who has overflowed with wisdom. (14)
He is the one who pierces with the weapon of wisdom. || 13 ||
The True Dharma is the King of Dharma, radiant, the light of the world, and the creator of the world. || 2 ||
The Lord of Dharma, the King of Dharma, the Master of Yoga, the Teacher of the Path. || 14 ||
He whose purpose is accomplished, whose resolve is fulfilled, and who is free from all conceptual constructions.
The element free from conceptual construction is the inexhaustible, supreme, and imperishable realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu). 15.
He is meritorious, a mass of merit, wisdom, and a great mine of wisdom; he possesses wisdom, is a true knower, and is fully endowed with the two accumulations. || 16 ||
In the eternal [state], Viśvarādya and others are the objects of longing; he is the one to be meditated upon, the protector of the intellects through meditation.
He is the one who exerts effort, the compassionate one, the consumer of offerings, the supreme delight, and the wearer of the three bodies. || 17 ||
The Buddha is the essence of the five bodies; the Knower is the essence of the five wisdoms;
his crown consists of the essence of the five Buddhas, and he upholds the union of the five syllables.

Janaka spoke these words to all the Buddhas: "O son, behold this state: it is wisdom, it is existence, it is the flow, it is devoid of phenomena, free from becoming, and the end-maker of existence. (19)
The sole refuge of wealth, the self-born, Sadyojāta, the protector of the world, Gaganodbhava, Bhava, Svayambhū, wisdom, the great light of knowledge. || 20 ||
Vairocana is of great radiance; Virocana is the manifestation of gnosis; he is the lamp of the world, proclaimed as gnosis, possessed of great splendor, and luminous. || 21 ||
The queen of mantras, the mantra-king who accomplishes the great purpose, dwells in the village of the forest-king.
He is the one who has transcended all pride, he is the delighter of the modest, the beholder of the universe, and he who moves beyond the sky.
He is the embodiment of the speech of all Buddhas, whose eyes bring joy to the world.
The creator Viśvarūpī also granted boons to the sage Puṣkara.
The mantra practitioner who wears the three lineages and upholds the great samaya.
The bearer of the Three Jewels, the most excellent, the teacher of the supreme vehicle. || 24 ||
Amoghapāśa, the Victorious One, Vajrapāśa, the Great Seizer.
The goad is the *vaṃja*, the great noose is the *vajra*, and he makes *Vajrabhairavī* his handmaid. || 25 ||
With the *Suviśuddhadharmadhātu*, there are twenty-five verses.
The six-faced one, fierce with wrath, possessing six eyes and a row of six arms.
With fangs, a terrifying skeleton, and a hundred faces like the Halāhala poison. || 1 ||
O Yamāntaka, subduer of obstacles, Vajraveśa, the terrifying one!
He whose thunderbolt is radiant, whose power is the thunderbolt, whose illusion is the thunderbolt, and whose great belly is the thunderbolt.
The Lord of the Vajra, the Conqueror, is like the center of the vajra-maṇḍala.
Lord of the thunderbolt, with a mass of matted hair, wearing an elephant hide as a garment;
he who utters "Hā hā" and "Mahāghora," and who is terrifying with the cry of "Hī hī."
Aṭṭahāsa, Mahāhāsa, Vajrahāsa, and Mahāvara. || 4 ||
Vajrasattva, Mahāsattva, Vajrarāja, Mahāsukha.
Vajracaṇḍa, Great Delusion, Vajrahūṃkāra, the Performer of Hūṃ. || 5 ||
The wielder of the thunderbolt, the bearer of the army, the one with the thunderbolt-sword, the cutter asunder.
The wielder of the universal vajra, the one who is without fear, the solitary vajra-holder, the conqueror of battle. || 6 ||
His forehead is like a thunderbolt; his hair is like the essence of the meaning of the thunderbolt.
He is the penetration of the thunderbolt, the great penetration, possessing a hundred-edged vajra-eyes. || 7 ||
His body was covered with a single hair on each pore, each hair being like a sprout of a diamond.
With a vajra-like firmness, his skin was dense with the essence born of meditation.
The glorious one who wears a garland of vajras, adorned with vajra ornaments;
he whose roar is the great laugh "Hā Hā," the vajra-thunder.
Ḍa and ca [are elided]. || 9 ||
O you of melodious voice, O great roar, O Lord of the three worlds, may you be our great protector!
The best among those possessing and lacking sound, [his voice] extends to the limits of the realm of space. || 10 ||
The ten verses on the knowledge of the mirror-like [wisdom].
Thus, let there not be the roar of the son of a barren woman— a proponent of emptiness— who desires the enjoyment of the supreme wheel of the reality-limit of non-self. (17)1.
The great-sounding conch of Dharma, the great drum of Dharma.
The drum of the Dharma resounds in all directions, proclaiming the non-abiding nirvana.
Herein is the hero, sharp-pointed like a thunderbolt, manifold in form, and consisting of mind.
The glorious one who manifests all forms, the bearer of the reflection of the moon.
He is unassailable, the great flame, the lord of the three worlds, and the Great Lord.
For the sake of awakening, one stands upon the path; what is this Dharma of great exaltation? || 4 ||
The three worlds, the quarters, the youths, the elders, the Buddhas, and Prajāpati.
Possessing the thirty-two marks, wearing the saffron robes, he was the most beautiful person in the world for the sake of Kāntakī.
The teacher of qualities who knows the world, the teacher of the world, free from false speech.
The three worlds were shaken by that sound, and the enemies were struck with fear.
The expanse of the sky is the enjoyment of the body; it is the enjoyment of the omniscient wisdom.
He is the one who destroys the snare of existence by means of the medicine of non-attachment.
Having pacified the ocean of saṃsāra, which is filled with the mud of afflictions, he has reached the further shore.
Crowned with the consecration of primordial wisdom, he is adorned with the ornaments of the perfectly awakened ones.
In the eighteen-fold cutting of the three poisons, there is no end to the mind; thus, liberation exists as infinite.
Completely liberated from all obscurations, with limbs equal to space. || 9 ||
Transcending the stains of all afflictions, you have gone beyond the paths of existence.
The great naga among all beings, who has destroyed the peak of the mountain of ignorance. || 10 ||
Freed from all limiting adjuncts, he is well-established in the path of the ether.
The great jewel-treasury of the Vinaya, the supreme among all jewels, is like a flash of lightning. || 11 ||
The excellent great auspicious jar emerged from the trunk of the great Kaśyapa tree.
He is the performer of what benefits all sentient beings, the seeker of their welfare, and the one who is affectionate toward sentient beings.
He knows the auspicious and the inauspicious, he knows the proper time, he possesses equal wisdom, and he is a knower of the right occasion.
He was one who knew the true nature of the faculties of sentient beings and was skilled in the three types of mastery. || 13 ||
He is virtuous, a knower of qualities, a knower of dharma, praiseworthy, and a source of auspiciousness for the world.
He is all auspiciousness, the source of auspiciousness, fame, renown, glory, and virtue.
A great festival, a great sigh of relief, a great bliss, and a great delight.
Honor, hospitality, the ground [of success], joy, prosperity, fame, and effort. || 15 ||
The protector, the bestower of boons, the most excellent, the friend, the supreme refuge, the destroyer of great fear, the enemy of enemies, the remover of the fear of withering. (19) 16.
He who has a crest, who wears a peacock feather, who has matted hair, who has a shaven head with matted locks, and who is adorned with a crown.
He has five faces, five tufts of hair, and five heroes as his crest-ornament.
Wearing the great vow, the sacred girdle, and the bark garment, he is the supreme ascetic.
He was a great ascetic, devoted to austerity, a snātaka, and a preeminent leader among those of the Gautama lineage.
The destroyer of obstacles, the one who has destroyed [all] obstacles, he who has attained the destruction of obstacles;
the liberator from bondage, the one liberated from the limbs of bondage, liberation, peace, and auspiciousness. || 19 ||
Nirvāṇa, cessation, peace, the state beyond fear, and the ender.
The ultimate end of pleasure and pain is dispassion, which is the destruction of all mental afflictions.
Unborn, unmanifest, without appearance, and stainless.
He is pure, all-pervading, omnipresent, subtle, the seed, and imperishable.
Free from dust, stainless, immaculate, free from the afflictions of wind, and without disease.

Well-awakened from the awakened state, he is the omniscient one, supreme among all-knowers; he has transcended the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), bears the form of the vehicle of wisdom, is free from conceptual construction, and is effortless. He is the perfectly awakened one who performs the Buddha-activities, without beginning or end, the primordial Buddha, without causal succession.
He is the single stream of wisdom, the embodiment of great gnosis—the Tathāgata. (20, 24)
Lord of Speech, great debater, king of speakers, preeminent among disputants.
The most excellent among those with faces, the supreme one, the lion among debaters, was defeated.
Samantadarśin, Prāmotha, Snehomālī, and Sudarśana.
He bears the Śrīvatsa mark, is well-spoken, is radiant with splendor, and possesses hands like lotuses. || 26 ||
The supreme and most excellent one among great buffaloes, he is the destroyer of the night-maker (the moon).
He is the man who is the wheel of all medicines without exception, and the great enemy of the disease of the afflictions.
The beloved Tilaka of the three worlds, the illustrious one from the circle of the Śrutis.
The ten directions were filled with water; he made the banner of Śarman his own. || 28 ||
The three realms proceed like a vast mandala of the nature of loving-kindness.
The glorious lord of the Ṛk-verses, the great observer, shall eat tomorrow. || 29 ||
The Great King Sarvabuddha, who maintains the embodiment of all Buddhas,
is the great yoga of all Buddhas.
The sole teaching of all Buddhas. || 30 ||
The Vajra-rakta-abhiṣeka (the Empowerment of the Red Vajra).
The glorious lords of all Vajra sovereigns.
Lord of all the lords of the world, sovereign of all who hold the vajra. || 31 ||
The great wheel of all Buddhas, which brings all under control.
(21) Nor is there any destination.
The great body of all Buddhas, the Sarasvatī of all Buddhas. || 32 ||
The great light of the sun of the forest, the stainless radiance of the moon of speech.
At the beginning of the pause is Mahārāga, with the luster of a child of the Viśvavajra. || 33 ||
He is the Buddha seated in the vajra posture, the Buddha who upholds the assembly and the Dharma;
he is the glorious one who approaches the Buddha, the omniscient one who upholds the skill in primordial wisdom.
The great King Viyodhana was a sustainer of universal illusion.
Vajrartī is the primordial great void, pure and the supreme syllable. || 35 ||
The great weapon of the Dharma, the vajra of the Mahāyāna that covers over suffering.
Having awakened the mind of enlightenment through fearlessness, he has fulfilled all the perfections; he is the sovereign who adorns all the stages.
He is a temple of pure Dharma, having descended into perfect knowledge.
The great lord of the abode of Māyā, the supreme sovereign of all mantras.
He who possesses the body of residual gnosis, having completely transcended all vajra-postures. || 38 ||
Samantabhadra, Sumati, Kṣitigarbha, and Jagadutpatti.
The great embryo of all Buddhas, whose face is the manifold emanation, the eternal one. || 39 ||
He is the totality of all things, the one who upholds the intrinsic nature of all existents.
He whose purpose is the welfare of the universe has the nature of non-arising; he upholds the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
Steadfast, with a perfectly serene nature, he is the Perfectly Awakened One who upholds enlightenment.
He is directly perceived by all Buddhas; he is the light of gnosis, supremely radiant. || 42 ||
The forty-two verses on the wisdom of discernment.
It is the supreme means for accomplishing one's desired goals and the purifier of all faults.
The Lord, the supreme among all sentient beings, the liberator of all sentient beings. || 1 ||
O hero in battle against the afflictions, you are the destroyer of the pride of the enemy that is ignorance.
He is wisdom, the bearer of erotic sentiment, the glorious one, the hero, and the possessor of a terrifying form.
With hundreds of arm-staffs cast about, he danced with the planting of his feet.
The illustrious Chatruja, whose dance is the enjoyment of the womb of Ga-ga, has awakened. || 3 ||
Standing upon the surface of the earth’s orb with one foot, he rests with the toe-nail of his other foot pressing against the peak of the cosmic egg.

The meaning of phenomena is twofold: the conventional and the ultimate; the object consists of various representations, and consciousness remains as a continuum of cognitions established upon the objective field. (5)
One who delights in the meaning of all phenomena without exception, delights in emptiness, and possesses supreme intelligence.
And having transcended the passion for existence and so forth, he is the great delight of the three realms of existence. (23) || 6 ||
Pure, bright, and white as a conch shell.
Possessing a splendor as pure and beautiful as the autumnal moon.
He has the luster of the orb of the rising sun and the natural radiance of great passion.

Oṃ, to you whose nature is the purity of all conditioned phenomena, equal to the ocean of space, pure by intrinsic nature, and surrounded by the Great Vehicle, svāhā! || 26 ||

O best of givers, there is no ocean like you; O lion-faced one, you have attained your state through the power of giving. May the compassionate one, who rejoices in the excellence of generosity, enter this city for its fulfillment.
In the Śāla forest, no dogs are found; only lions have attained the Śāla grove. And what sound is there for a dog that enters the den of a lion? It is a cry of distress.
In the absence of power, there are no Buddhas; they do not attain the realization of the Dharma.
Even those who have reached the state of lions among men, possessing patience and compassion, do not hear the sound of one entering into the vast expanse of the compassionate ones.

The Buddha is endowed with the power of vigor; like a lion, he has reached the limit of vigor. Through the mastery of his vigor, the sound of this compassionate one resounds as he enters among the gods.

The Buddha is not possessed of the power of meditative concentration alone; these lions among men have attained the power of meditative concentration. Through the power of meditative concentration, the Compassionate One hears the sound of his own son as he enters his own city.

The Buddha is endowed with the power of wisdom; indeed, wisdom has been attained by that Lion among Men. By the power of his wisdom, the sound of the Compassionate One is heard as he enters his own city.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Aparimitāyurjñānasuviniścitatejorāja.
Namely: Oṃ pūṇāt mahāpūṇya aparimita pūṇā aparimitāy-pūṇāhmana saṃbhāro pacita.

Oṃ, all conditioned phenomena are utterly pure; to the assembly of the Tathāgatas, who are equal to the self-nature of purity, through the fulfillment of the Great Way, svāhā! Thus spoke the Blessed One. And those monks, those bodhisattvas, and that entire assembly—gods, humans, asuras, garuḍas, and gandharvas—rejoiced at what was spoken by the World-Honored One. The Noble Aparimitāyur-nāma-dhāraṇī, the Mahānaya Sūtra, is completed.
(46) The Mahāyāna sūtra entitled the Aparimitāyur-nāma-dhāraṇī is completed.
"Those phenomena," and so forth.
In the year 970, the illustrious Narasiṃha, son of Dhīra, established this [image] of Śrī Bhāja at Cāyātapoya.
Where is the one who sacrifices with laughter? || ||
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed Noble Prajñāpāramitā!
Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.

In the Jeta Grove, O Lord, the great community of monks was present, fully complete with four hundred monks, together with a multitude of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who had donned the great armor. There were one hundred thousand Bodhisattvas,
all of whom were irreversible and had correctly entered upon the path.
Namely as follows:
By Mañjuśrī as a youth, by Āryaprayoga, by Asaṅgapratihāra, and by Anikṣiptadhura.
Thus, together with twelve hundred thousand bodhisattvas, the youth Mañjuśrī then, at that very time,

departed from his own residence made of emerald and approached the residence of the Tathāgata. Having approached, he stood outside the gate of the residence in order to see and attend upon the Tathāgata.
Then Śāradvatīputra also, having emerged from the Skandhāvāra monastery, approached the Tathāgata’s monastery in order to see, pay homage to, and attend upon the Blessed One.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana also [did so].
Venerable Mahākāśyapa; venerable Mahākauṣṭhila.
And all the other great śrāvakas as well.
Each went to his own monastery, departed from there, and approached the monastery of the Blessed One; having approached, they entered it.
Then the Blessed One, having recognized that the assembly of the great disciples had arrived, emerged from his own dwelling and went outside to a secluded spot near the monastery.
He sat down on the very seat that had been prepared. Having sat down, the Blessed One, knowing [the time], did not address you, Śāradvatīputra.
Having arrived at the door of the Tathāgata’s vihāra, he stood there crying out, "Kṛtāṃśa! When he had been addressed in this way, the venerable Śāradvatīputra said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, you should first of all address Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta."
It is indeed true that Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta spoke thus to the Blessed One:
"So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata. Having first of all arrived at my own dwelling, I went forth from it and approached the dwelling of the Tathāgata.
Having approached, I stood to one side, desiring to see and pay homage to the Blessed One."
For what reason? Because, Blessed One, I am not yet satiated by the sight of the Tathāgata, nor by saluting him, nor by attending upon him;

and even when I approach the Tathāgata for the sake of seeing him, saluting him, and attending upon him, it is for the benefit of all sentient beings. Therefore, Blessed One, the Tathāgata is to be seen, he is to be saluted, and he is to be attended upon.
Such is his substance;
such is he worthy of being saluted, as I perceive him to be worthy of being honored with offerings.

"In whatever way I pay homage and in whatever way I attend upon [the Tathāgata], in that very same way the Tathāgata becomes visible, having been honored and attended upon. And I, for the sake of all sentient beings, behold the Tathāgata. The Blessed One said: "Mañjuśrī, how is the Tathāgata to be seen, and even how is he to be attended upon?"
Mañjuśrī said:
I behold the Tathāgata through the aspect of suchness; I behold the Tathāgata as one who is non-conceptual, whose nature is non-arising, and who is thus characterized by non-origination.
I behold the Tathāgata through the aspect of being without any form;
yet suchness does not go anywhere.
Thus do I see the Tathāgata: suchness neither comes into being nor passes away;
thus do I see the Tathāgata.
Suchness does not abide in a location, nor does it abide in a particular place; thus do I see the Tathāgata.
Suchness is neither past, nor future, nor present; thus do I perceive the Tathāgata.
Suchness is not characterized by duality, nor is it non-dual;
thus do I perceive the Tathāgata.
Suchness is neither defiled nor purified;
thus do I perceive the Tathāgata.
Suchness does not arise, nor does it cease.
In this way I behold the Tathāgata;
in this way the Tathāgata becomes seen,
saluted, and attended upon.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Mañjuśrī, the Youthful:
“Mañjuśrī, look in this way; what do you see?”
Mañjuśrī said:
"Seeing thus, O Blessed One, I do not see anything at all.
Seeing thus, O Blessed One, I do not perceive the arising of any dharma,
nor do I perceive its cessation."
Then the second son of Śara, Prathāyu, spoke thus to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
O Mañjuśrī, you are a doer of what is difficult, in that you behold the Tathāgata as being without measure.

Thus, while he dwells in close attendance upon all sentient beings, he has set out in great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) toward them; yet there is no conceit regarding any sentient being, nor any attachment to the notion of a "sentient being," and he is engaged for the sake of the final nirvāṇa of all sentient beings, without any attachment to the notion of a "sentient being. He exerts himself for the sake of all sentient beings, having donned the armor and girded his loins with the yoga of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), up to and including the yoga of non-application (*ayoga*).
When this had been said, the youth Mañjuśrī addressed the venerable Śāradvatīputra: "So it is, Venerable Śāradvatīputra; it is exactly as you say.
This armor is donned for the sake of the parinirvāṇa of all sentient beings. Yet, O Venerable One, there is no apprehension of a sentient being here, nor is there any attachment to a sentient being."

Śāradvatīputra, don the armor! Thus armored, how could I cause a deficiency or a fullness in the realm of sentient beings? Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, if for the sake of conceptualization, in each and every buddha-field there were [Buddhas] as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā...

Suppose there were as many Buddhas, Blessed Ones, as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, and each Tathāgata were to remain for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, teaching the Dharma day and night; and suppose that by each of those teachings of the Dharma,

as many sentient beings were disciplined by those Buddhas, Blessed Ones, as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, such that each Tathāgata, through each single teaching of the Dharma, would discipline that same number of sentient beings— and having done this for every single one of them, not even a single sentient being would be perceived as either deficient or full within the realm of sentient beings.

"For what reason? Because of the non-existence of sentient beings and because of the isolation of sentient beings. Venerable Śāradvatīputra, since neither decrease nor fullness is perceived in the realm of sentient beings," when this was said, the venerable Śāradvatīputra spoke thus to the youth Mañjuśrī:
"If, Mañjuśrī..."
Because it is non-differentiated from you, neither decrease nor increase is perceived in the realm of sentient beings.
Therefore, who now shall show you that Dharma which you have fully awakened to?
When this had been said, the youthful Mañjuśrī spoke thus to the venerable Śāradvatīputra:
Since, O Śāradvatīputra, you are thus self-controlled and have completely transcended all sentient beings, whom will you honor, or to whom will you give the Dharma?
For what reason is that so? Because, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, all phenomena are ultimately devoid of conceptual proliferation.
Then indeed, the Blessed One spoke thus to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
Since, Mañjuśrī, all phenomena are ultimately non-existent, why then do you now seek to cause them to be perceived through wisdom?
Moreover, Mañjuśrī, if some being were to ask you, "What is a sentient being?", what would you say to him?
Mañjuśrī said:

"O Blessed One, I would ask her this: 'Blessed One, if all the Buddha-dharmas are thus being sought, what is the measure of the wisdom of beings, such as Pūtana, Pitṛ, and Cchatrika? O Blessed One, I would ask her this and say: 'What is the measure of the domain of the Buddhas?'"
The Blessed One said: "Indeed."
Having completely cut off.
(53) Mañjuśrī, when you have been questioned by anyone at all, answer that person.
"What is the basis for the suffering of sentient beings?
Tell me what its nature is."
Mañjuśrī said:
O Blessed One, when she asks me this, I would speak thus: "That which is the inconceivability of the non-arising of all phenomena."
The Blessed One said: "It is so."
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, if someone were to ask you, "Upon what is the realm of sentient beings established? what would you say to him?
Mañjuśrī said:

In that regard, O Blessed One, I would ask anew and say this: "Is the realm of non-arising established in the realm of sentient beings, or is it unestablished? The Blessed One replied: [It is unestablished].
Mañjuśrī, at whatever time you cultivate this perfection of wisdom, where do you establish yourself when you cultivate the perfection of wisdom?
The Play of Mañjuśrī.
At whatever time, Blessed One, I cultivate the perfection of wisdom, at that time, Blessed One, I cultivate the perfection of wisdom while being non-abiding.
The Blessed One said: "Mañjuśrī, you have replied that for one who is established, it is precisely that cultivation of the perfection of wisdom which consists in non-abiding anywhere."
The Blessed One said: "Mañjuśrī, at whatever time you cultivate the perfection of wisdom, at that time your roots of merit either increase or do not decrease."
Mañjuśrī said:
"Blessed One, at that time, does any root of merit undergo accumulation or diminution?
Blessed One, such a person does not cultivate the perfection of wisdom."
For whatever phenomenon there may be, whether it is an increase or a decrease.
That perfection of wisdom, Blessed One, is not to be understood as a cultivation.
Whoever is established in the condition of either the increase or the decrease of any dharma whatsoever.
O Blessed One, that perfection of wisdom, through its very cultivation, does not abandon any phenomena whatsoever.

Nor does he destroy the Buddha-dharmas. Why is that? Because, Blessed One, the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is not established by way of apprehending any dharma whatsoever, such that he might destroy any dharma through his wisdom.
O Blessed One, that is indeed cultivation which does not perceive the faults of saṃsāra as distinct from the qualities of nirvāṇa.

For what reason? Because, Blessed One, I do not perceive even cyclic existence itself, so how could I speak of it? I do not apprehend even nirvāṇa as having the defects of cyclic existence, so how could I speak of it? And I am unable to perceive even the qualities of nirvāṇa. (55)

Thus, for one who practices the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom, O Blessed One, there is neither grasping nor abandoning, neither taking up nor laying down. For one who practices the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom, O Blessed One, there is neither the increase nor the decrease of any phenomenon, even of nirvāṇa. Why is that? Because, O Blessed One, that which is non-arising is neither increased nor diminished; that which is the cultivation of this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
Therefore, Blessed One, that cultivation of the perfection of wisdom does not produce or cease any dharma.

Blessed One, that cultivation of the perfection of wisdom does not bring about the deficiency or the fullness of any dharma. Blessed One, such is that cultivation; indeed, Blessed One, such is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Blessed One, the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is that which does not seek even those phenomena that are formless; it is not partial, nor indeed, Blessed One, is it something to be realized or perceived, because it is sought right where there is nothing to be sought. Such is the cultivation of the Blessed One’s perfection of wisdom, such is the cultivation of the Blessed One’s perfection of wisdom: "These phenomena have been seen by wisdom; these phenomena are supreme; these phenomena are foremost. (56)
One does not perceive phenomena as something distinct from oneself.
Of those phenomena, there may arise the state of being carried toward the summit.

Thus, O Kūpa-putra, through the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom, one does not find any dharma whatsoever; O Blessed One, the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom does not obstruct any dharma, nor does it cause deficiency.

Therefore, Blessed One, since there is no production of a person, nor of the beginningless suchness, nor of the true nature of phenomena, up to all dharmas— whatever is the non-production of these, Blessed One,
that is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
Thus, O Blessed One, the glory of the state of a youth (kumārabhūta) is proclaimed;
yet, Mañjuśrī, the supreme qualities of a Buddha are not [attained] thereby.
Mañjuśrī said:
"Blessed One, because they are ungraspable, the Buddha-dharmas are ungraspable.
Therefore, Blessed One, it is not a contradiction for the Tathāgata to declare that all dharmas are empty."
The Blessed One said:
In this very way, Mañjuśrī, all phenomena have been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata as empty.
Mañjuśrī said:
Furthermore, does the Blessed One perceive any superiority or inferiority within emptiness?
The Blessed One said:
“Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī! It is just as you have said, Mañjuśrī.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, the Buddha-dharmas are not sequential.”
Lord Mañjuśrī!
"Is it thus, Blessed One? Are the Buddha-dharmas not indeed immortal?"
For what reason, Blessed One, is it that one does not encounter any phenomena whatsoever, nor perceive them, nor apprehend them? Because the qualities of a Buddha are thus.

Furthermore, Blessed One, this cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is the mother and progenitor of the qualities of a Buddha, because it leads to their attainment; it is the relinquisher of the qualities of ordinary worldlings, because it leads to their abandonment.
Thus, Blessed One, through the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom, one understands that even the slightest phenomenon is non-existent and devoid of intrinsic nature.
The Blessed One said:
O Mañjuśrī, you do not disparage the Buddha or the Dharma.
Mañjuśrī replied: "No, Blessed One. It is not possible for me to fully comprehend the perfections of the Buddha-dharmas without the complete cultivation of the Blessed One’s perfection of wisdom."
"These are the dharmas of ordinary persons; these are the dharmas of śrāvakas; these are the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas; these are the dharmas of perfectly enlightened buddhas."

For what reason? Because, Blessed One, when a son of good family is devoted to the practice of yoga in the cultivation of this very perfection of wisdom, he does not point out the dharmas of ordinary persons among these dharmas, nor does he point out the dharmas of the Śrāvakas,
nor does he point out the dharmas of the Arhats.
If one were to point out the dharmas of a perfectly awakened Buddha, I do not perceive any such dharmas here.

Thus, O Blessed One, the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is the Blessed One’s cultivation of the perfection of wisdom. Having practiced the course of cultivation, it occurs to a son of good family as follows:
"This is the realm of desire, this is the realm of form, this is the formless realm; this is the realm of cessation."

For what reason? Because, Blessed One, I do not perceive any phenomenon whatsoever that has cessation as its nature. Thus, Blessed One, the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom should be understood as follows:
the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom, Blessed One, does not bring about benefit or harm to any phenomenon whatsoever.
Indeed, Blessed One, the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is neither a giver of the qualities of a Buddha nor a destroyer of the qualities of an ordinary person.
In this very way, there is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom as it truly is:
that which is the cessation of the phenomena of ordinary persons is not the attainment of the phenomena of a Buddha.
When the Blessed One had spoken thus, the youth Mañjuśrī addressed him in this way.
Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī! It is well that you thus teach such a profound Dharma.

This has been revealed by you, Mañjuśrī, for the sake of the penetration of reality as it truly is for those bodhisattvas who are great beings, for those śrāvakas who are conceited, for those who have fallen away from the path, and for those who belong to the lineage of bodhisattvas—for the penetration of reality as it truly is for those śrāvakas who are conceited, for those who have fallen away from the path, and for those who belong to the lineage of bodhisattvas. Mañjuśrī, there are sons of good family or daughters of good family...

Indeed, they will have attended upon many Buddhas and planted roots of merit under many Buddhas before hearing this exposition of the Perfection of Wisdom by Gomitra; otherwise, how could they not be terrified or fall into despair? Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, it is only those who have planted roots of merit under hundreds of thousands of Buddhas who will hear this.
Then, having heard this profound teaching on the Perfection of Wisdom, the venerable Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One,
may the Blessed One further elaborate upon this teaching of the Perfection of Wisdom."
"It occurs to me, Mañjuśrī," the Blessed One said.
Mañjuśrī said:
Blessed One, it should be understood that this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom for these [beings].
She who has approached for the sake of instruction in any dharma whatsoever.
Why is that? Because, Blessed One, all phenomena are indeed without support; such is their cultivation.
Furthermore, Blessed One, that which is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is that in which one does not perceive any phenomenon whatsoever as being either defiled or purified.
Such, Blessed One, is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
“With apprehension, Blessed One, is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom. With apprehension, Blessed One, is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.”
Then the Blessed One addressed the youth Mañjuśrī: "Mañjuśrī, how many Tathāgatas have you seen?"
They have resorted [to them].
Mañjuśrī said:
To whatever extent, Blessed One, the mind and mental factors of an illusory person are pure.
"O Blessed One, so many Tathāgatas have been attended upon by me."
The Blessed One said: (61) bha.
Mañjuśrī, you are not established in the Buddha-dharmas.
Mañjuśrī said:
Furthermore, Blessed One, is any dharma to be found that does not abide within the Buddha-dharmas?
The Blessed One said:
But to whom, Mañjuśrī, do these Buddha-dharmas belong?
Thus spoke Mañjuśrī.
Since even for the Blessed One these so-called "Buddha-dharmas" do not exist, how much less could they possibly exist for anyone else? How then will they ever come to be?
The Blessed One said:
"Has it been attained, Mañjuśrī? Mañjuśrī replied, "It has been attained."
"O Blessed One, I shall indeed fashion them; what more need I say? I shall approach you with my mind focused."
The Blessed One said:
“Why then, Mañjuśrī, are you dejected? Mañjuśrī replied: “The seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa), Mañjuśrī.”
The Blessed One has descended from the jewel of enlightenment attained through newness; how then shall I abide, having made the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) my standard?
The Blessed One said:
“O Blessed One, ‘the limit of reality’ is a designation for the view of a self-existent body.”
The Blessed One said:
With what intention, Mañjuśrī, do you say this?
Mañjuśrī said:
It is not so, Blessed One. The body is not a non-existent body; it does not transmigrate, yet it is not a non-existent body.
Then the venerable Śāradvatīputra said this to the Blessed One:

"To what extent, Blessed One, will those bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, exist who, having heard this teaching on the perfection of wisdom, will have faith in it, will not be discouraged, and will not shrink back?
Then indeed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya said this to the Blessed One:

They were silent, O Blessed One. Those bodhisattvas who, having heard this exposition of the perfection of wisdom, will have faith in it, and who do not shrink back, do not tremble, and do not fall into terror—they will become great, indeed very great, for the sake of awakening.
Therefore, O Blessed One, it is precisely this non-comprehension of these phenomena that is, without cause or reason, the supreme awakening.
Then Mañjuśrī, the youthful prince, addressed the Blessed One in this way.
O Blessed One, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who study this perfection of wisdom for the sake of vision are indeed Buddhas; they will not fall into a state of exhaustion.
For what reason? Blessed One, "Buddha" is a designation for the ultimate non-arising. Then, O Blessed One, Nirañjanā addressed him thus:
"Blessed One, those bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas will not surpass ordinary phenomena, the phenomena of śrāvakas, the phenomena of pratyekabuddhas, or the phenomena of perfectly awakened buddhas;

having heard this teaching on the perfection of wisdom, they will not have conviction in it, they will not believe in it, they will not find confidence in it, and they will not attain composure. For what reason? Because, Blessed One, all phenomena are without conflict (*asaṃvāda*), since they do not exist; therefore, there is no conflict for them, nor does it exist."
Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Śāradvatīputra: "It is so, Śāriputra; it is just so."

Śāradvatīputra, if a son of good family were to abide for non-retrogression in the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), and if, Śāradvatīputra, the Blessed One had not fully awakened to the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), then that very realm of ordinary persons would have been established as the ultimate reality.
Moreover, Śāradvatīputra, this very dharma-sphere is awakening.

Then, for what reason? Because all phenomena (dharmas) are the undifferentiated realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu). When one is established in the awakening that "all phenomena are the realm of phenomena," they proceed by way of calculation [realizing] that this very realm of phenomena is the object of the Buddha, because all phenomena are the domain of the Buddha due to their momentary diversity.
"O Venerable Śāradvatīputra, 'non-differentiation'—this is a term for that which is non-informative; what is informative? "O Venerable Śāradvatīputra, it is not possible to know that."

"Is it by way of being conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) that you speak of making known (*vijñāpayituṃ*), or is it by way of being unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)? In that regard, there is no making known at all; therefore, it is without making known (*avijñaptika*). Venerable Śāradvatīputra, all phenomena (*sarvadharmāḥ*) are without making known.
Why is that? Because there is no manifestation (*prādurbhāva*) of any phenomena whatsoever."
Abiding in which they would recite [the mantra]:
those who are thus empowered are empowered by the inconceivable; they are empowered by the inconceivable, empowered by the real.
For what reason? Venerable Śāradvatīputra, this state is the state of non-conceptualization, the state of non-differentiation.
Those who are endowed with the inconceivable do not go to heaven, nor do they go to rebirth, nor do they go to final nirvāṇa.

For what reason? Because they do not exist as something established by way of going or coming in the inconceivable, up to and including not existing as something established by way of going or coming in final nirvāṇa. Thus it was said, O Venerable Śāradvatīputra, regarding those established in the four roots of merit.
Therefore, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, one does not indeed seek the root of the self at the root of the self. It is difficult to perceive.
"O Bhikṣu, 'rootless' is a designation for one who is unestablished.

Having superimposed the notion that what has arisen is a 'designation' (adhivacana) and a 'means' (karaṇa), Venerable Śāradvatīputra becomes worthy of offerings in the world. For what reason? Because such a dispersal is a further superimposition."

"Venerable Śāradvatīputra, a monk who possesses faith does not deserve to consume what has been given out of faith; rather, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, a monk who lacks faith deserves to consume what has been given out of faith.

Venerable Śāradvatīputra, a monk whose conduct is improper does not deserve to consume what has been given out of faith; rather, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, a monk whose conduct is proper deserves to consume what has been given out of faith."
Śāradvatīputra, a monk whose vision is unimpaired is called an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted. O! (66)
With what intention, Mañjuśrī, do you speak thus?
Mañjuśrī said:

“Venerable Śāradvatīputra, it is with reference to this—that which is the equanimity that has completely destroyed non-equanimity and is the very essence of equanimity—that ‘one whose outflows are exhausted’ (kṣīṇāśrava) is a designation for an Arhat. Śāradvatīputra said:
"But with what intention, Mañjuśrī, do you speak thus?
Mañjuśrī replied:
The fears of one who drinks poison do not subside.
By that much he will be liberated.
"Venerable Śāradvatīputra, it was with this in mind that I said: 'One who has crossed over fear' is a designation for an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted.
Śāradvatīputra asked: "Mañjuśrī, of what is 'one who possesses the patience of the unarisen' a designation? Mañjuśrī replied:
Venerable Śāradvatīputra, he by whom non-arising dharmas have not been produced is called one who possesses the patience of the unarisen.
Śāradvatīputra said:
"Mañjuśrī, for whom is the term 'undisciplined monk' a designation? Mañjuśrī replied:
"Venerable Śāradvatīputra, 'disciplined monk' is a designation for an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted."
Why is that? Because he has been disciplined by the discipline of terrors; he is one who was undisciplined before being disciplined.

Of what is this a designation? "Buddha"—he who has not come from anywhere, who has not arisen, and who will not pass away. Since he is not endowed with even a single dharma, there is not even a single word here that can be differentiated; this, O Śāradvatīputra, is the designation for what is called "Buddha. Venerable Śāradvatīputra, one who wishes to seek the Tathāgata should seek the self. "Self," Venerable Śāradvatīputra, is a designation for that which absolutely does not exist and is not to be found.

In the same way, the Buddha also does not exist at all and is not apprehended. Just as the self cannot be designated by any dharma whatsoever, so too the Buddha cannot be designated. It is not easy, Reverend Śāradvatīputra, to understand this designation "I am," just as it is not easy to understand the designation "the Buddha. Reverend Śāradvatīputra, it is not easy to understand the designation "the Buddha" when it is used as a conventional expression.
Then, indeed, the venerable Śāradvatīputra said this to the Blessed One:
"Lord,
this Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta does not teach in the manner that a beginner bodhisattva who is to be trained would understand."
When this had been said, the youthful Mañjuśrī addressed the venerable Śāradvatīputra as follows:
"Venerable Śāradvatīputra, I do not teach in such a way that those who have committed offenses will understand it, nor do I teach it as an Arhat."
Just as space will not cognize anything, for what reason is there no awakening?
Some things have not been known by the Fully Awakened One, nor seen, nor heard, nor remembered, nor produced, nor ceased, nor hated, nor taught.

To this extent, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, is awakening; yet that awakening is neither a being nor a non-being. For what reason? Because nothing at all has been fully awakened to by means of awakening, nor does awakening fully awaken to awakening.
Śāradvatīputra said:
Homage to Mañjuśrī, who is perfectly awakened as the Dharma-realm of the Blessed One.
Mañjuśrī said:
Venerable Śāradvatīputra, the Blessed One has not fully awakened to a dharma-realm.

Why is that? Because, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, the Blessed One is himself the dharma-realm. Sons of good family and daughters of good family who hear this teaching on the perfection of wisdom will not be terrified, will not be frightened, and will not fall into a state of terror regarding awakening and liberation.
And those who receive it with a mind full of faith, Śāradvatīputra, will become supreme lords of giving, great lords of giving, and distinguished lords of giving.

Śāradvatīputra, those who, having heard this teaching on the perfection of wisdom, have attained the path of ethical discipline and develop resolute conviction, and who do not tremble, do not become terrified, and do not fall into terror— they, Śāradvatīputra, will be endowed with supreme faith, supreme vigor, supreme meditative concentration, and supreme, unimpeded wisdom.
Śāradvatīputra, those bodhisattvas will become endowed with the knowledge of omniscience, which is possessed of all the supreme aspects of the seasons.
Those who, having heard this exposition of the perfection of wisdom, will have faith in it, and will not be terrified, nor frightened, nor fall into terror—[they shall attain supreme enlightenment].

Furthermore, the Blessed One said this to the youthful Mañjuśrī: "Mañjuśrī, what is your own nature? Do you desire your own perfection, or do you wish to fully awaken to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment?"
Mañjuśrī said:
If I were to awaken, O Blessed One, I would desire this very great awakening for myself; yet, O Blessed One, I do not seek awakening for my own sake.
"For what reason? Because, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, you are a bodhisattva who has long practiced this.
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī! It is well that you desire these profound sūtras."
"Just as you have previously not made any claim regarding non-apprehension and the crossing over,
Mañjuśrī said: 'O Blessed One, if I were to practice non-apprehension, then the Dharma would be something acquired.'"
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the youthful Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Do you see these, Mañjuśrī? "I do not see them, Mañjuśrī," he replied.
Do you understand, Blessed One?
The Blessed One said:
Why do you speak thus?
Mañjuśrī said:

Thus, O Blessed One, I see in such a way that I do not perceive ordinary persons, nor do I perceive those beyond training, nor do I perceive those both trained and untrained, nor indeed do I perceive anything at all.
I see it thus.
I do not see what I have never seen before, nor do I see what I have already seen; I do not perceive what is disciplined, nor do I perceive what is undisciplined.
Then the venerable Śāradvatīputra said this to the youthful Mañjuśrī:
“Mañjuśrī, since you do not view those who belong to the vehicle of the śrāvakas in such a way, how then do you view those who belong to the vehicle of the perfectly enlightened ones?”
Mañjuśrī said:
"O Venerable Śāradvatīputra, regarding the term 'bodhisattva,' I do not perceive such a name, nor do I perceive any dharma that has fully awakened."
Thus, venerable Śāradvatīputra, I do not see anyone belonging to the vehicle of the perfectly awakened ones (samyaksaṃbuddhayānika).
Śāradvatīputra said:
Mañjuśrī, since you are a Tathāgata, how can you be later?
Mañjuśrī said:
Let alone, O Bhayankara Śāradvatīputra, [the others]; let the Nāgas subdue the Great Nāga.
When this had been said, the venerable Ārya-Śāradvatīputra addressed the youth Mañjuśrī:
"Mañjuśrī, what is the designation for 'Buddha'?"
Mañjuśrī said:
Furthermore,
venerable Śāradvatīputra, Mañjuśrī said: "This, 'non-arising,' is a synonym for that."
"Regarding 'the purified self,' Mañjuśrī said: 'It is so, O Venerable Śāradvatīputra; for whomsoever that which is called "self" is non-existent, [for them] it is thus.'"

(72) The designation for that is "Buddha. However, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, this term "Buddha" is a designation for the non-existent; it is not possible, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, to make known by means of words that which is called "Buddha."
"Furthermore, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, speech is neither a pig nor a form; why then, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, do you say such a thing?
This is my intention, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, when I say this: 'Disciplined' is a designation for a monk who is an Arhat, one free from taints."
Śāradvatīputra said:
"‘He chooses what has been chosen’—of whom, Mañjuśrī, is this a designation?
Mañjuśrī replied:
"O Venerable Śāradvatīputra, 'one who wanders in what has been appropriated' is a designation for an ordinary person."
Śāradvatīputra said:
"With what intention, Mañjuśrī, do you speak thus?
Mañjuśrī replied, "For it is so, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, that even awakening is empty."
When this had been said, the venerable Śāradvatīputra spoke thus to the crown prince Mañjuśrī:
"Excellent, excellent! Mañjuśrī, you speak just as one whose faculties are undiminished would speak.
Mañjuśrī replied:
(73) It is exactly as you have said, Venerable Śāradvatīputra. He is one whose outflows are exhausted, an Arhat. For what reason? Because, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, my outflows are exhausted.
The stage of the śrāvaka is liberated, and the stage of the pratyekabuddha is liberated; by this method, O Venerable Śāradvatīputra, one is neither a śrāvaka nor an arhat.
Then the Blessed One said this to the youth Mañjuśrī:
"Mañjuśrī, it might be that there is a way in which a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having sat down at the seat of awakening, would not fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Mañjuśrī replied:

"Could it be, Blessed One, that by way of a synonym, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are called 'those who have sat at the seat of awakening' because they have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"

Why is that? Because in awakening, not even a minute dharma is found; therefore, it is unattainable and cannot be spoken of as "unsurpassed perfect awakening. And that awakening has indeed not arisen; therein, not even a single dharma is found—by what could it be perceived? That which is awakening is non-existent, and by that non-existence, awakening is seen.
By means of which he awakened to enlightenment, or by that very enlightenment he awakened, as far as the seat of enlightenment— therein he shall remain.
"By this method, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the youth Mañjuśrī:
"O Mañjuśrī, to whom does this designation 'enlightenment' refer?"
Mañjuśrī said:
"O Blessed One, 'awakening' (bodhi) is a designation for these three vehicles."

Why is that? Because, in this way, the five aggregates have the nature of awakening (*bodhiprakṛti*). Since they are not connected, this awakening is not connected; since it is not connected, it is not bound. Awakening is not the cultivation of the six sense bases; awakening is the emptiness of all phenomena. Why is that? Because all phenomena are directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*) by their very nature; they are not to be fully awakened to by anyone, nor are they known through the knowledge of non-abiding. This awakening is indeed not something to be known, yet it was indeed fully realized by the Blessed One in the past.
These have been consecrated by him and bound together, as far as they have been made manifest.
When this had been said, the Blessed One, Mañjuśrī the Youthful, spoke as follows.
Mañjuśrī, it occurs to me in this way: "The Tathāgata is my Tathāgata."
Mañjuśrī said: "No, indeed, Blessed One. Why is that? Because, Blessed One, it would not be for me that there is a Tathāgata, nor that I am a Tathāgata."
Why is that? Because suchness is just as it is, and because suchness is not otherwise than suchness;
for, Blessed One, a Tathāgata does not make known a Tathāgata by means of that which is not suchness.
The Tathāgata does not make known suchness.

For what reason? Because, Blessed One, from the perspective of ultimate truth, suchness is non-existence. Since the Tathāgata is non-existence, it would follow for us that the Tathāgata is merely suchness. Furthermore, [the term] "Tathāgata" [is used in this sense].
"Blessed One, this is merely a name; how could that Tathāgata exist where such a thing as this will come to pass?"
"The Tathāgata is my Tathāgata."
The Blessed One said:
Your doubt, Mañjuśrī, has been removed by the Tathāgata.
Mañjuśrī said:
"No indeed, Blessed One; there is no doubt. Whether the Tathāgata is present or whether the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, the splendor of the Tathāgata remains the same.
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the youth Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
Nata, Mañjuśrī, it is precisely thus that the Tathāgata is said to have arisen.
Mañjuśrī said:
"O Blessed One, it might be that the Tathāgata does not exist, if he were to be subject to conceptual proliferation."
The Blessed One said, "Not so, Mañjuśrī; it is not the case that the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who have entered parinirvāṇa are as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā."
Mañjuśrī said:
"Is it the case, Blessed One, that the cognitions of the Buddhas have a single object, whereas the objects of the Blessed One's [cognitions] are manifold?"
The Blessed One said:
It is even so, Mañjuśrī; the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have but a single sphere, namely, the sphere of the imperishable.
Mañjuśrī said:
But, Blessed One, does anyone at all remain thus?
The Blessed One did not say so.
"It is so, Mañjuśrī," he said.
Therefore, Blessed One, these Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are like the sands of the river Gaṅgā;
they have entered final nirvāṇa.
For what reason? Because, Blessed One, the Buddhas, Blessed Ones, have manifold objects; that is to say, their objects are immeasurable.
And it does not arise or cease apart from the mind; therefore, Blessed One, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who will appear in the future have already awakened.
Why is that? Because these states of the mind are not past, nor future, nor present.
"O Blessed One, the arrangement of the worlds within that [egg] is vast."
“O Blessed One, they fall into conceptual proliferation regarding the appearance in the world of a Tathāgata, thinking: ‘A Tathāgata has arisen,’ or ‘He will pass into parinirvāṇa.’”
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the youth Mañjuśrī:

“Mañjuśrī, it is not that those Tathāgatas have thought of you or spoken of you; rather, you have uttered these words in the presence of the Tathāgata like a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who possesses the jewel, or like an Arhat, a Kṣīṇāśrava.”
For what reason? Because it is thus: for him, there is no "I," no "mine," and no ignorance.
They do not turn back at all.
Why is that? Because he has thus established himself and is firmly resolved.
Mañjuśrī said:
"O Blessed One, since all phenomena are neither permanent nor impermanent by their very nature, do they not transcend both acceptance and rejection?"
The Blessed One said: "Mañjuśrī, in the very same way that the Tathāgatas have made a determination, so too have ordinary persons made a determination.
Mañjuśrī said:
Ordinary worldlings, Blessed One, are likewise fixed in that very state.
The Blessed One said:
Thus it is, Mañjuśrī; for what reason? Because all things are eternal.
Mañjuśrī said:
For what reason did the Blessed One say this?
Just as the Tathāgata is neither annihilated nor eternal.

"In this way, even ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) are non-eternal. "Is it not so, Blessed One, that the state of being an ordinary person is also non-eternal? "For what reason? Because, Blessed One, all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are indeed eternal. Blessed One, those who have set out for parinirvāṇa are laughed at; Blessed One, for what reason? Those very ones who are non-eternal are the ones who, having set out for parinirvāṇa, are laughed at."

"Blessed One, for what reason is it that those who have attained certainty [regard] that very thing as final nirvāṇa? Therefore, Blessed One, regarding the lack of certainty, you have said: 'These are the qualities of ordinary persons; these are the qualities of the noble ones. To them, this should be said:
'Go first to spiritual friends and then, subsequently, you will know: "These are the qualities of ordinary persons; these are the qualities of the noble ones. "
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the youthful Mañjuśrī:
Mañjuśrī, you have seen the Tathāgata as the supreme [refuge] for all sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī said:
I desire, Blessed One, that the Tathāgata [teach] for all sentient beings; if there were here any sentient being who had attained final nirvāṇa.
The Blessed One said:
"Mañjuśrī, do you consider the Tathāgata to be endowed with impermanent phenomena?"
Mañjuśrī said:
I wish, Blessed One, that the Tathāgata were endowed with the quality of impermanence;
for if he were endowed with any quality of impermanence whatsoever, [he would not be the Tathāgata].
The Blessed One said:
"I wish that these disciples of mine, Mañjuśrī, were likewise disciplined by the Tathāgata.
Mañjuśrī said:
"I wish, Blessed One, that these disciples of mine were likewise trained by the Tathāgata."

If someone were to ask, "O Blessed One, is the arising of anyone's suffering or well-being caused by the favor or disfavor of another? one who knows discipline would answer him thus: "No, Blessed One. The arising of anyone's suffering or well-being is not dependent upon the favor or disfavor of another.

For what reason? It is because, in this way, this essence of the *dhātu* is unmixed with the *dhātu*; it is eternally the *dhātu*, and within that *dhātu* there is no diversity of Śrāvakas, up to and including ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
The Blessed One said:
"O Blessed One, it would be well if the Blessed One were to further explain the teaching on the Perfection of Wisdom, as Mañjuśrī desires.
"Mañjuśrī, let it be revealed to you," the Blessed One said to him.
Mañjuśrī said:
This, O Blessed One, is to be understood as the cultivation of that perfection of wisdom.
It is not prepared for the apprehension of any dharma whatsoever as an object.

For what reason? Because, Blessed One, all dharmas are indeed without an object (*anālambana*). Thus, Blessed One, the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is the cultivation wherein one does not follow after any dharma whatsoever—whether it be afflicted or purified—as being real or as being unreal.
In this way, Blessed One, is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
“O Blessed One, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
Then the Blessed One spoke thus to Mañjuśrī: “It has been attended upon by you.”
Mañjuśrī said:
Blessed One, as many mental states and mental factors as have ceased in the mind of an illusory person.
"O Blessed One, so many Tathāgatas have been attended upon by me."
Bha! (81) The Dharma-eye that had not yet arisen has now been purified.
Then the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and,
bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows:

“Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition for the appearance of this great trembling of the earth in the world? When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, this discourse on the Dharma called ‘The Exposition of the Field of Merit’ has been taught by previous Buddhas, Blessed Ones, in this very spot of earth. This, Ānanda, is the cause; this is the condition for the appearance of this great trembling of the earth in the world.”
Then, indeed, the venerable Śāradvatīputra said this to the Blessed One.
Is it not indeed because of the Blessed One Mañjuśrī’s perpetual fearlessness? For what reason is that so? Because, O Yakṣa, whatever appears to the Tathāgata appears as impermanent.
Then the Blessed One addressed the youth Mañjuśrī:
"It is even so, Mañjuśrī; it is just as Śāradvatīputra speaks. Whatever occurs to the mind of the youth Mañjuśrī, all that appears to him as being eternally so."
When he had thus been released, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta said this to the Blessed One:
"No, Blessed One, it does not appear as impermanent; rather, for me, it appears as impermanence itself.

Furthermore, Blessed One, whatever is slightly impermanent, all that sound is impermanent. There is no sound that is not impermanent; nor is there a sound that is not a sound, nor a non-sound, which can be designated by means of its power."
The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, you should enter the samādhi of the eternal."
Mañjuśrī said: "No indeed, Blessed One; I do not enter into a permanent meditative absorption, Blessed One."

For what reason? Because, Blessed One, I am indeed that inconceivable samādhi; I am this inconceivable samādhi, Blessed One, and I am inconceivable. "Blessed One, how can one enter into this inconceivable samādhi? "It is inconceivable, it is truly inconceivable. How then does one enter into the inconceivable samādhi? Furthermore, Blessed One, for one who has previously practiced the conduct of a beginner, the inconceivable samādhi is to be entered through the practice of the ocean-like conduct.
Thus [he said]:
"O Blessed One, now indeed this practice of the son of a king is prevailing; may I here enter into the concentration on impermanence."

It is just as, Blessed One, when a noble one who is a beginner on the stage of training has not yet mastered the piercing of a cow-hair, such a practice occurs to him: "Am I indeed like this [in my lack of skill]? But when he has become proficient in the piercing of the cow-hair, then that same practice arises in him again: "Am I perhaps still like this [cow-hair piercer]? This is because of his having been well-trained in the piercing of the cow-hair.
And yet, furthermore, whatever he desires or intends to pierce, that very thing he pierces with ease.
"In the same way, Blessed One, it occurred to me: 'May my conduct be entirely fulfilled; may I enter this concentration.
Then, having entered this concentration, I dwelt by means of this concentration.
At that time, even while merely being myself, it occurred to me: 'One should dwell by means of this concentration.'"
For what reason? Because whenever I dwell in this samādhi, [I am free from fear].
At each such time, this meditative concentration is merely a designation.
Then, indeed, the Venerable Śāradvatīputra addressed the Blessed One in this way.
For here, O Blessed One, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta has manifested as the universe.

“While dwelling by means of this ‘Impermanence’ concentration (*anitya-samādhi*), [the Blessed One] said: ‘O Blessed One, is there another concentration more peaceful than this “Impermanence” concentration? Then, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta said to the Venerable Śāradvatīputra:
‘How, Śāradvatīputra, do you conceive of that other “Impermanence” concentration as being peaceful?’”
Furthermore, as the Venerable Śāradvatīputra has said:

"Is there, from this inconceivable samādhi, another samādhi that is more peaceful? "Venerable Śāradvatīputra, is this inconceivable samādhi perceived or apprehended by you? If it were so, then there might be another samādhi from this inconceivable samādhi that is more peaceful. Śāradvatīputra said:
"For this, Mañjuśrī, is the 'eternal' samādhi; it does not exist and is not perceived.
Mañjuśrī said:
"In that same way, Reverend Śāradvatīputra, this 'eternal' samādhi is inconceivable; that samādhi neither exists nor is it perceived."
Furthermore, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, there are some who are seekers of the concentration on impermanence;
indeed, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, all sentient beings are seekers of the concentration on impermanence.
For what reason?
Because all that is impermanent is, by its very nature, impermanence;
this is the samādhi of impermanence. Therefore, all sentient beings have entered into this samādhi of impermanence.
Then the Blessed One addressed the youth Mañjuśrī.
