"Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī! It is well that you have spoken thus regarding all these profound points. Just as a being who has previously performed service for the Victors does not perceive a self, so too, Mañjuśrī, it is because one abides in the perfection of wisdom that you speak thus."
Mañjuśrī said:
If it were so, Blessed One, that by abiding in the perfection of wisdom one speaks thus.
Even so it would be: having approached for the sake of refuge, he spoke thus;
or, abiding in the perception of a self, he spoke thus.
Remaining within the perception of existence, he spoke thus.
Therefore, abiding in the perfection of wisdom, he spoke thus.
For what reason is that?
If, Blessed One, there were a fixed station for the perfection of wisdom, then the perfection of wisdom would not be without a fixed station.
Moreover, the station of the self-nature of rebirth is the station of the perfection of wisdom; it is a non-arising, a non-abiding, and not a state of stability.
Such a station is an impermanent station; it is not the station of any dharma whatsoever.

The place of the established doctrine is the place of the eternal, the place of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). O Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom is the non-arising of all phenomena. This perfection of wisdom is a designation for the realm of the unborn; that which is the realm of the unborn is the realm of non-arising; and that which is the realm of non-arising is the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). That which is the realm of phenomena is the realm of the ocean-like conduct.
The element that moves from the ocean with its own sound.
That which is the imperishable element (*akṣaya-dhātu*) is the self-element (*ātma-dhātu*);

and that which is the self-element is the perfection of wisdom element (*prajñāpāramitā-dhātu*). For this perfection of wisdom element and the self-element are non-dual; they are not divided into two. Therefore, this is the imperishable element. Thus it is said: "This is not..."

Because it is the element of permanence, therefore it is the element of non-arising; because it is the element of non-arising, therefore it is the element of the nature of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*); because it is the element of the nature of phenomena, therefore it is the element of signless conduct; because it is the element of signless conduct, therefore it is the element of non-conduct; because it is the element of non-conduct, therefore it is the element of permanence; because it is the element of permanence, therefore it is the element of self (*ātmadhātu*); because it is the element of self, therefore it is non-designation (*aprajñapti*).

(87) Because this element is the element of delight, it is the perfection of wisdom-element; because it is the element of the eternal, it arises from that which does not arise. That which does not arise is non-existent; that which is non-existent does not perish. Since it does not perish, it is eternal. Thus, the Tathāgata-element is such; and since this is non-dual and indivisible, the Blessed One said this regarding the unconditioned.
The perfection of wisdom is the cultivation of the self-nature; for what reason?
Because "perfection of wisdom" is a designation for the realm of the self (ātma-dhātu), O Blessed One.
For what reason?

Blessed One, one who would know the element of self (*ātma-dhātu*) would know the non-dual nature of phenomena (*dharma*); for what reason? Because that which is thus eternal is the knowledge of a Buddha, and for no one whatsoever are there dual phenomena.
The wisdom of the Śrāvakas is the wisdom of the Buddhas. For what reason? Because that wisdom does not exist in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).

That which does not exist in the ultimate sense—how could it set in motion the Wheel of Dharma? And when that wisdom does not exist in the ultimate sense, then that wisdom is non-attached; and when that wisdom is non-attached...
When non-arisen knowledge does not exist for the sake of existence, and when there is the existence of knowledge, then non-arisen knowledge will not exist;

[thus] knowledge is without objects. When that knowledge is independent, when that knowledge is mind-dependent, when that knowledge is unestablished, then that knowledge is established; then that knowledge is neither produced nor [ceased].
Even when attained, it does not appear.
For what reason? Because that knowledge is neither refined by qualities nor unrefined by qualities.

For what reason? Because that knowledge is established as being eternally free from both qualities and defects. Since that knowledge is free from conceptualization (*niścinta*), therefore that knowledge is eternal. That very knowledge which is thus known—by means of the yoga of non-apprehension and by means of that unarisen knowledge—no phenomenon whatsoever has been fully awakened to by it; nor has anything arisen prior to that knowledge, nor has anything come from the future limit (*aparānta*). Nor is that knowledge produced, nor was it produced in the past;
it is neither beginningless nor endless, neither finite nor infinite, and it will neither perish nor stand still.
There is no other knowledge whatsoever that is similar to that knowledge; therefore, that knowledge is incomparable.
Nor indeed does its beginning, middle, or end appear when that [object] is situated in knowledge;
therefore, that knowledge is like space.
Whether the strength of that barber is equal or unequal,
that knowledge of his is not equal; for another knowledge is found to be a counteragent even to the knowledge of that barber.
Therefore, that knowledge is not commensurate with reality.
Then indeed, the Blessed One spoke thus to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, that gnosis is not something that can be diminished."
Mañjuśrī said:
"O Blessed One, this was not done; therefore, this is not an offense."
It is just as if, Blessed One, there were an unstruck sound from this [instrument].
Just as when one adds a small amount of ash to base metals, they do not come to be reckoned as base metals,
even so, Blessed One, this gnosis— unmade, unaccumulated, unproduced, unarisen, and ceased— is not to be reckoned as base metal. Then the Blessed One addressed the youth Mañjuśrī:
O Mañjuśrī, when this teaching on the knowledge of the Tathāgata has been thus explained, you will have faith in it.
Mañjuśrī said:
Blessed One, those who do not perceive phenomena as being subject to saṃsāra,
nor as being subject to parinirvāṇa,
they have resolute conviction.

Those who have not shaken off the view of a self-existent body (*satkāya*), whose greed, hatred, and delusion are not exhausted—for what reason is there no exhaustion for them? They do not reach exhaustion; they do not transcend cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), nor do they enter the count of those in cyclic existence.
Thus, while manifesting a perception of the path as being full of flavors, they do not understand the meaning of what has been spoken.
Then the Blessed One spoke to the youth Mañjuśrī: "Mañjuśrī, at that time, he spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva."

“Excellent, excellent, O wise counselor! Your well-spoken words are indeed like a triple chariot. Furthermore, in this world, O Mahākāśyapa, you have not spoken in vain. Then the venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed the Blessed One as follows: “Blessed One, it will be so; Subhūti has spoken in accordance with the Dharma and Vinaya of the Tathāgata, and in accordance with the Perfection of Wisdom.”
O virtuous ones, you are those who cross over, those who possess resolute conviction, those who have attained full knowledge, and those who accept [the teaching].
When Tāreśvara had finished speaking, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda:
"Ānanda, right here in this assembly of monks, there are laymen and laywomen who have approached;
they are unable to fathom this profound Dharma and Vinaya, nor can they penetrate this profound Prajñāpāramitā."
They will become saviors, possessors of resolute wisdom, those who have fully understood and accepted [the truth],
and they will be renowned as deliverers. Just as, for example, a priceless jewel—
such as a *piṇḍa* or a *mākaṣṣapa* or a *gṛhapati*— is highly valued by its weight in gold, so too is this jewel of the mind, which is stainless and beautiful.

(91) When one has thus resolved in the mind, one becomes happy and filled with joy; one is free from anxiety and without mental preoccupation. In the same way, Kāśyapa, when monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen hear this Perfection of Wisdom—which is unborn, unarisen, and by nature in a state of final nirvāṇa—they will not fall away from their existence. Listen and pay close attention!
It will pierce.

"How is it that this very profound Perfection of Wisdom, which is unborn, unproduced, and established by its very nature, up to its being non-existent—having heard of it at another time, they will become joyful, happy, with their minds free from distress and discursive thought, and they will speak these words: 'Alas, we were not able to see the Elder; alas, we missed the opportunity for his instruction! For we did not encounter that Perfection of Wisdom which is unborn and unproduced, nor did we hear of its non-existence.'"
Just as the Pārijāta tree, when it has grown and flourished, will not long remain small,
but will become the largest of all trees,
so too, Kāśyapa, the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen who have heard this profound Perfection of Wisdom being taught and proclaimed will become joyful and delighted in their hearts.

"Kāśyapa, those who will hear this profound Perfection of Wisdom—which is unborn, unarisen, and non-existent until its very end—and who, having heard it, will have joyful and gladdened minds in the future, they shall go to that [state]. Those who were not present here in this assembly, but who will have joyful and gladdened minds in the future—for them, through the power of their mental joy and gladness, the Pūrnika flower will soon come into bloom; and all that was given by all the Buddhas will reach full fruition."

"Kāśyapa, this profound perfection of wisdom, which has been proclaimed and has arisen, will remain and circulate even after the passing of the Tathāgata. In the future time as well, Kāśyapa, it should be understood that this is through the empowerment of the Buddhas and by the majestic power of the Buddhas."

For what reason is that, Kāśyapa? Because these profound *prajñāpāramitā* teachings have never before been heard by those who have not previously generated the aspiration for awakening. For example, Kāśyapa, suppose a jeweler, upon seeing a precious gem, becomes overjoyed;
one should not conclude from this that it is his first time seeing such a precious gem, for he has seen it many times before. In the same way, Kāśyapa, regarding this profound [teaching]...

"Kāśyapa, those who speak these words— 'The Perfection of Wisdom, as far as it has been born or produced, shall, by its heroism, cause the leaders to be joyful, delighted, glad, elated, and filled with joy and happiness; their fame shall spread far and wide'— these, Kāśyapa,
are those who have previously attended upon Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta when he was teaching this exposition of the Perfection of Wisdom, namely, that 'all things are unborn and unproduced.'"
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, suppose a certain person were to go from a village to a city or a town for some business, but having gone there, he did not return.
Then, at a later time, someone else might approach him and describe the excellence of that city.

They, having heard of the beauty of those regions, the beauty of the countryside, the beauty of the lotus ponds, the beauty of the groves, the beauty of the springs, fountains, and lakes, and the beauty of the flowers and fruits, would speak of them with joy; and having heard them, they would find satisfaction and,
being filled with gladness, would further entreat him.

"O Devatā, having proclaimed this person as 'a carrier' (*vaha*), he becomes one who has reached the goal; for by this person, [the path] was previously prepared. He shall go there to those delightful regions, the delights of the countryside, the delights of the lotus ponds, the delights of the gardens, the delights of the springs, lakes, and groves, and the delights of the flowers and fruits. Why is that?
Because, having heard that, his soul becomes satisfied, and supreme joy and gladness arise within him."
In the same way, Kāśyapa, when Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta has been questioned, he will respond with the knowledge of the future, and his speech will be perfectly nourished and complete.
(95) Having heard this profound Prajñāpāramitā as it was spoken and produced, he will experience a sublime joy; he will experience a sublime joy; he will attain a sublime joy.
Speaking these words, that deity said: "We have heard exactly what was taught regarding the Prajñāpāramitā, namely, that all phenomena are unborn and unproduced."
When this had been said, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke thus to the Blessed One:

"Blessed One, these faithful sons and daughters of good family will, in the future time, at a later period, become renunciants possessing the three knowledges (*traividya*). These have been prophesied by the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Kāśyapa; it is exactly as you have spoken.

In the future, there will be sons of good family and daughters of good family who are faithful, devoted to the welfare of others, and who will become like images cast from a mold, just as those whom I have designated here and now."

Then Mañjuśrī, the youthful prince, addressed the Blessed One in this way: "Blessed One, that Dharma is without form and beyond reach; yet, Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom—even up to its being called 'without darkness'—possesses forms. How can there be forms, signs, and measures for that which is thus described?"

And since the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dharma is without form, without marks, and without signs, how, Blessed One, will there be a designation of the form, mark, and sign of that which is formless, markless, and signless?
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the youth Mañjuśrī:

“Mañjuśrī, these very forms, tokens, and signs of those sons of good family and daughters of good family will come to pass, who, when this Perfection of Wisdom—which is neither existent nor non-existent, unarisen and untaught—is being taught, shall have faith in it and even cause others to write it out.
For, Mañjuśrī, by the illumination of the Perfection of Wisdom, the illumination of all the Buddha-dharmas is to be seen.”

Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, the manifestation of the impermanence of reality should be seen as follows: while you were practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva in the past, you accumulated roots of merit through impermanent roots of merit, and thereby attained the realization of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

Therefore, a son of good family or a daughter of good family who wishes to accumulate roots of merit should hear this very perfection of wisdom, have faith in it, write it down, recite it, master it, and explain it to others.
It should be studied, recited, mastered, properly attended to with the mind, and cultivated.

To whatever extent one has flowers, incense, garlands, ointments, worship, excellent parasols, banners, bells, flags, lamps for victory and fame, and offerings, one should worship with such honors according to one’s ability and according to one’s strength.

A son of noble family or a daughter of noble family who desires to surpass the stage of all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas should honor this Perfection of Wisdom, having heard it nine times, to whatever extent they are able.
Just as, Mañjuśrī, the sun emerges from the ground of the ravivākṣika.

In this way, Mañjuśrī, a son of good family or a daughter of good family who wishes to hear, and indeed to practice, all the teachings spoken by the Buddhas through their equality with non-arising, should hear this perfection of wisdom; they should practice it, Mañjuśrī,
if they desire the full awakening to all the qualities of a Buddha.

O Mañjuśrī, whether it be a son of good family or a daughter of good family who wishes to have faith in this teaching, even though all dharmas have not yet been fully realized by the Tathāgata, they must hear this Perfection of Wisdom, and so on, up to honoring it. They must hear this very Perfection of Wisdom, and so on, up to honoring it, even if they are overwhelmed by the corpse of a son or a daughter.

Furthermore, O Śāriputra, this very perfection of wisdom should be heard and mastered by a son of good family or a daughter of good family who desires to attain the state of liberation, and by a son of good family who desires to give rise to the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) with firm resolve. There is no other dharma whatsoever that is superior to this. Therefore, one who wishes to realize this very meaning and goal should indeed apply themselves to this perfection of wisdom.

Or, whether it be a son of good family or a daughter of good family, this very perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) should be heard and mastered. For there is no other dharma whatsoever that is superior to the thought of awakening (bodhicitta). Therefore, a son of good family or a daughter of good family who desires to hear and master all dharmas without conceptualizing them, should hear and master this very perfection of wisdom. Why is that? Because this is the perfection of wisdom.

Whether it be the perfection of any phenomenon, its production, its destruction, or its manifestation— since all phenomena are neither defiled nor purified— a son of good family or a daughter of good family who desires to act in this very way must listen to and practice this very Perfection of Wisdom.
A son of good family or a daughter of good family who has faith in all phenomena—past, future, and present—must certainly listen to and practice this Perfection of Wisdom.
Why is that? Mañjuśrī, non-arising is neither past, nor future, nor present.
Why is that? Mañjuśrī, because all phenomena have non-arising as their refuge.

In this way, for those who have cut through all doubts regarding all phenomena, a son of good family or a daughter of good family who desires [this], by whom it has been heard, by whom it has been studied, and by whom it has been mastered according to the manner of Mañjuśrī—
so that he may become one who turns the wheel of the Dharma, which has three revolutions and twelve aspects—

one who desires its destruction, one who desires to establish himself therein, one who has resolute faith therein, or one who desires to practice it, [that] son of good family or daughter of good family [should listen]. (100)

O son of good family or daughter of good family, by one who desires to treat all sentient beings with loving-kindness, by one who desires to abandon the perception of "sentient being," by one who desires not to dispute with the whole world, by one who desires not to quarrel with the whole world, and by one who desires to awaken to the non-attainment of the whole world—this very Perfection of Wisdom must be heard, and so forth, until it is honored. It is for one's own welfare that this very Perfection of Wisdom must be heard, and so forth, until it is honored.

Furthermore, a son of good family or a daughter of good family who wishes to awaken to the non-arising of all phenomena as they truly are must train in this very perfection of wisdom by means of the yoga of non-apprehension.
Then Mañjuśrī, in the form of a youth, addressed the Blessed One as follows:

O Blessed One, for the Perfection of Wisdom which is devoid of qualities, what is its essence? O Blessed One, for the Perfection of Wisdom which is characterized by nothingness, which is neither arising nor perishing, which does not bring about any dharma, which does not exclude any dharma, which is motionless, inactive, and effortless, and which—failing to perceive an intrinsic nature and seeing no intrinsic nature—is the giver of no dharma whatsoever, what is its essence? (101)

All phenomena are neither to be made selfless nor to be made with a self; all phenomena are neither makers of unity nor makers of multiplicity. Of that which is uncreated, inexhaustible, and non-expansive—of the phenomena of ordinary beings, of Pratyekabuddhas, of Bodhisattvas, and of Buddhas—the three bodies are the body of gnosis, the body of non-duality, the body of non-departure, and the body of no cyclic existence.

For those who obstruct the path to liberation, who destroy the qualities of a Buddha which are free from obstruction, who cause the decay of the body, who act as disturbers and agitators, who are contrary to all dharmas, who are antagonistic, who obscure, who are according to their own names, who act with effort, who act with separation, who act with detachment, who act with compassion, who act with duality, and so on up to those who are non-existent— [for all such people...]

The Blessed One said this to the youth Mañjuśrī: "Mañjuśrī, such are the qualities and such are the benefits of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) that should be understood by you. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva who wishes to train in the bodhisattva-samādhi and wishes to produce the miraculous power of a bodhisattva—by abiding in which samādhi—"

If one wishes to see all the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and their Buddha-fields; if one wishes to know their names; if one wishes to perform the unsurpassed worship of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones;
and if one wishes to apply oneself to their teaching of the Dharma and to have faith in it—one should train here in this very Perfection of Wisdom through the application of training.
Then Mañjuśrī, in the form of a youth, addressed the Blessed One as follows:
For what reason, O Blessed One, is this called the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said:
"Mañjuśrī, it is called the perfection of wisdom because it is unarisen and because there is no awakening;
that is to say, because it is primordially peaceful and because it is without a refuge."
Because it is not to be done;
because it is as long as the day.

Non-existence is this perfection of wisdom. For this reason, Mañjuśrī, one should not expect the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom from bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas. And this is the domain of these bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas: that which is the domain of all phenomena. Moving within this, Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva, mahāsattvas, becomes intent upon the domain and does not fall away.
Thus, this sphere of activity is the sphere of all the Mānikas; therefore, because it was made an object of entry by Akṣayamati, this very sphere is called "the non-sphere" (agocara).
Then, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta addressed the Blessed One.
"Bhagavān, where does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwell so that he will swiftly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening?"
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Mañjuśrī, the Youthful:
“Mañjuśrī, practice this perfection of wisdom; a bodhisattva mahāsattva who does so will swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
The *astimuñja* is the concentration named *śrī-ekatyuha*; by means of this concentration, a bodhisattva mahāsattva will quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
When this had been said, Mañjuśrī, the youthful prince, spoke thus to the Blessed One.
"How, Blessed One, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva enter the *ekavyūha* concentration? For what reason is it called the *ekavyūha* concentration?"
The Blessed One said:

"Ekavyūha"—this is a designation for the non-arising (*anutpāda*) of Mañjuśrī. A son of good family or a daughter of good family who wishes to enter the *ekavyūha* samādhi should first of all thoroughly examine the *prajñāpāramitā*;
thereafter, they will enter the *ekavyūha* samādhi.
For what reason? Mañjuśrī, non-arising is unshakable;
it is not subject to anger, cannot be provoked to anger, and is beyond conceptualization.
It is not to be cultivated through discursive thought.
Mañjuśrī, a son of good family or a daughter of good family who wishes to enter the meditative absorption of the single array after having resolved upon it should prepare various seats.
They should take delight in solitude and remain without attending to any signs; sitting cross-legged, they should bring to mind a single Tathāgata therein.
All phenomena should not be brought to mind.
By way of non-apprehension, one should call upon this Tathāgata and take up his name.
Having heard and apprehended that name, from whichever direction [it comes]—(105)
The Tathāgata sits facing me; you should direct your attention toward that very Tathāgata.
By not neglecting him, the Blessed Buddhas of the past, future, and present will have been attended upon by you.

For what reason? Because, Mañjuśrī, this quality of a Tathāgata is one: just as for a single Tathāgata there are immeasurable Buddha-qualities and immeasurable eloquence, even so, Mañjuśrī, by attaining this *ekavyūha* samādhi—

A single person shall expect and proclaim a specific, immeasurable variety of Dharma-discourses, which have been spoken by the Arhats, the Pratyekabuddhas, and the Perfectly Awakened Buddhas, and as many of those Dharma-discourses as have been preserved in this world, so many will manifest to him. Thus, having established this single array of meditative concentration, he shall teach the Dharma with its causes and foundations until the end of his lifespan.

Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, as for those certain bodhisattvas who belong to the lineage of bodhisattvas and who think, "What is this single array samādhi?", they should not speak thus. Rather, they should take up and abide by this proclamation of inconceivable qualities that has been proclaimed; they should take up and abide by it in such a way that you may perceive the qualities of this samādhi exactly as they have been taught according to the prescribed method, and you should practice accordingly.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, it is not possible through this samādhi alone to fully accomplish [the goal], because of the various views—such as the view of self, the view of a living being, and so forth, up to the view of existence. For example, Mañjuśrī, suppose there were a man who possessed a priceless, incomparable jewel. Someone might say to him:
"What is this? O man, are these the immeasurable qualities of that jewel? Then, indeed, that man would explain the meaning of that jewel to him.

"O man, suppose you had this jewel-gem; you would know how to polish it. Then, O man, having taken that jewel-gem, you would have it polished by a skilled polisher. Once that jewel-gem has been polished, it would become worthy of being weighed."
To whatever extent one causes that mani-jewel to be polished,
to that same extent one perceives the qualities of that mani-jewel.
In this very way, Mañjuśrī, whenever a son of good family or a daughter of good family enters into such a meditative absorption,
they will not perceive even the six seasons as they pass by.
Mañjuśrī, it is like this: suppose there were some man who, having been pierced by the rays of the sun, was tormented by them.

In the very same way, Mañjuśrī, having attained the concentration of the single path (*ekayāna-samādhi*), one does not teach the Perfection of Wisdom as the teaching of any particular dharma whatsoever in empty space. In this very way, one sees all dharmas as unarisen and unceasing.

Mañjuśrī, it is as if there were four men who, having crossed over the great ocean named Nadapavyāpin, which is eighty-four thousand yojanas in extent, were to taste its water. Mañjuśrī, all of that would have a single flavor, namely the flavor of salt; in the very same way, Mañjuśrī, whatever Dharma teaching I have taught has but a single flavor, namely the flavor of non-arising, the flavor of non-existence, the flavor of liberation, and the flavor of cessation.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, a son of good family established here in this samādhi teaches the Dharma with this very flavor.

All that, Mañjuśrī, he teaches as having but a single flavor: the flavor of non-arising and non-ceasing, the flavor of existence, the flavor of dispassion, the flavor of liberation, and the flavor of cessation. Having attained this samādhi, O noble son, whoever desires to teach the Dharma should teach it in this way.
He should speak, explain, and instruct thus:

"For in this way, Mañjuśrī, noble son, having attained this samādhi, whatever teaching is given—whether concerning all phenomena, all beings, or all entities—it will not be taught falsely, nor will it be taught erroneously. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, by relying on this samādhi, a bodhisattva mahāsattva will quickly fulfill the qualities that lead to awakening and will very swiftly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva mahāsattva will awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment once he no longer conceptualizes the self-element (*ātma-dhātu*) up to the phenomenon-element (*dharma-dhātu*) in terms of arising, nor in terms of cessation, unity, or plurality. In this way, Mañjuśrī, even a momentary bodhisattva mahāsattva will quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, provided he does not think of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment as something to be attained.
For that son of good family, there is the attainment of these bodhisattva qualities, and he is one who has set out for the realization of awakening and buddhahood.

Mañjuśrī, I declare that this son of good family will swiftly attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment through such patience. One who resolves thus—that all phenomena are the Buddha-dharmas—and does not waver from it, I also declare to be irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
and he should be said to be never separated from all the Buddha-dharmas.
"If, upon hearing this exposition, a son of good family or a daughter of good family here were not to become stiff-necked or envious," [so it was said].
When this had been spoken, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Bhagavān, from what cause is unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment produced?"
The Blessed One said:
"No, Mañjuśrī, it is not so; nor is it produced from the cause of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

Why is that? Because there is neither arising nor non-arising, nor is there anything produced from a cause. For what reason? Because all phenomena are unborn. Therefore, Mañjuśrī, for whichever son of good family or daughter of good family here—"
Having heard this exposition, one should not become despondent;
I declare that such a person is irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī, when this profound perfection of wisdom is being taught, whether it be a monk, a nun, a layman, or [a laywoman]—(110) 1)—
Or,
Mañjuśrī, whatever sons of good family or daughters of good family do not enter into the assembly until they have gone for refuge to me and have been ordained by me here— I am their teacher. 2)

In this profound perfection of wisdom, that which is not taught is not a training in which a bodhisattva trains. Mañjuśrī, it is just as, for example, whatever seeds of grain, sprouts, or plants grow in the great earth, they all do so depending upon the great earth; even so, Mañjuśrī, whatever wholesome roots belong to bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, they all, being embraced by the perfection of wisdom, attain growth, expansion, and development, and they lead to the non-deceptive, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
When this had been said, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One,
regarding this teaching on the perfection of wisdom which has been taught by the Blessed One, is there anyone [who can grasp] this teaching on the perfection of wisdom of the Blessed One?"

"In the villages, towns, or districts of this Jambudvīpa, they will become well-restrained. When the Blessed One had finished speaking, he addressed the youth Mañjuśrī: 'Mañjuśrī, those who, having heard this very teaching on the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā), have conceived a firm resolve, thinking, "In this way we shall hear the teaching on the Perfection of Wisdom even after passing through various births"—they will hear it, and they will cultivate it extensively. "

"Mañjuśrī, those who have not cultivated [the roots of virtue] and whose roots of wholesome merit are weak, yet who, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, experience a great joy and exultation upon hearing it—Mañjuśrī, one who wishes to hear this teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā* should be addressed thus: 'O son of good family, do not be like a gambler; having heard even a mere portion of it, do not fall into despondency because of a lack of faith.'"

Why is that? Because the perfection of any dharma whatsoever has not been seen; neither the non-arising, nor the destruction, nor the attainment of the dharmas of ordinary beings has been taught; nor has the arising, nor the destruction, nor the attainment of the dharmas of those beyond training, nor of the dharmas of the Pratyekabuddhas been taught. When this had been said, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Lord, if at any time a monk, a nun, a layman, or a laywoman should speak thus: 'I have personally beheld the profound practice of the perfection of wisdom;
form is empty, emptiness itself is form; form is not separate from emptiness, and emptiness is not separate from form.'"
In this way, Śāriputra, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty.

Thus, Śāriputra, all phenomena are empty of their own specific characteristics; they are unproduced, unceasing, undecaying, immovable, stainless, and neither deficient nor complete. Therefore, Śāriputra, because of emptiness, there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness; no eye, no ear, no nose, no tongue, no body, and no mind; and no forms.

There is no sound, no odor, no taste, no object of touch, and no mental phenomenon (*dharma*). There is no eye-element, and so on, up to the element of mental phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). There is no exhaustion of ignorance, no exhaustion of passion and hatred; no suffering, no origin, no cessation, and no path. There is no knowledge, no attainment, and no non-attainment.

Therefore, Śāriputra, because there is no attainment, Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, dwell relying upon the perfection of wisdom; because it is merely a mental object, they have transcended to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and have reached Nirvāṇa, being separated from the three times by all the Buddhas. Furthermore, through the perfection of wisdom, they have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Therefore, Śāriputra, it should be known from this very fact.

The Prajñāpāramitā mantra, the great vidyā-mantra, the unsurpassed mantra, the unequaled mantra, the mantra equal to the peerless, the mantra that pacifies all suffering, which was proclaimed by the Blessed One after meditating correctly on the perfection of wisdom, is as follows: Tadyathā: [om gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā]
Oṃ gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā.
In this way, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should apply himself to this most profound perfection of wisdom.
Then the Blessed One, having emerged from that samādhi, gave his approval to the noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, saying, "Excellent!"

"Excellent, excellent, son of good family! It is even so; that which has been taught in this profound *prajñāpāramitā* is approved by all the Tathāgatas. Thus spoke the Blessed One. And the Venerable Śāriputra, the noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, and all those present—the world of gods, humans, asuras, garuḍas, and gandharvas—rejoiced and were delighted by the words of the Blessed One. [End of Chapter Twelve]
The Noble Dhāraṇī of the Perfection of Wisdom in Twenty-five Verses is completed.
"Ye dharmā" and so forth.
Oṃ, homage to the Mother, the Noble Prajñāpāramitā!
Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain,

surrounded by a great community of monks numbering many hundreds, and by many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas, headed by Śakra, the lord of the gods, and many hundreds of thousands of millions of gods and humans, headed by the world-protectors.
The Blessed One, Śrīratnagarbhasiṃhasena, taught the Dharma.

In the lotus, the eyelashes, blood, mutual benefit, the awakening of the lamp of knowledge, at the time of your arrow, the compassionate weeping, sin, and the singular liberation.

Oṃ, homage to the Lord of the World! Homage to you, the Bodhisattva, the Mahāsattva, the ascetic;
to the noble Avalokiteśvara, the Great Lord, the one of sublime glory. (1)
Salutations to Śaṅkara, who is adorned with lotus-glories, who bestows the speech of the True Dharma, and who is the leader for those whose vision is the world. || 2 ||
To the one who always bestows the supreme gift of consolation to the world, who possesses hundreds of thousands of hands and millions of eyes; (3)

To the one whose face extends as far as the submarine fire (Vaḍavāmukha), who is the leader of the quarters beginning with the moon (the north), who conforms to all dharma, who is dear to dharma, and who is pure; || 4 ||
Salutations to the one who brings about the great liberation of all sentient beings from suffering;
salutations to the lotus-born one, whose name is the consolation for those like me.
Salutations to the one whose limbs are filled with the mass of wisdom, who bestows the beloved fruits of dharma and artha,
who is adorned at his feet by the glory of jewels, and who grants the fortune of the three goals of life.
To the one who causes the drying up of all the grounds of hell,
who is resplendent with the glory of wisdom, and who bestows the splendor of knowledge.
Salutations to the one worshipped by the worlds including the gods and the lords of the asuras; salutations always to the one who has been praised and saluted by his devotees. (174) 8.
To the one who teaches the perfection of the gift of fearlessness, to the radiant Sun-like Illuminator, the lamp-maker of the Dharma. || 9 ||

To the one who can take any form at will, the Gandharva of beautiful form, the most handsome; to the one mounted upon the mind, who dwells in the realization of the ultimate truth; to the one whose nature is profound Dharma, and who grants face-to-face vision; to the one who has attained all meditative absorptions, and who brings an end to the cycle of existence. || 11 ||

To the one whose limbs are sprinkled with wisdom, who possesses a body like that of the Bull among Sages, and who effects the complete liberation of those bound by the bonds of increasing attachment; 12.
To the one who acts in accordance with all beings, who is endowed with [all] perfections, who is like a wish-fulfilling gem in beautiful form, and whose retinue is like a mountain of jewels. || 13 ||
To the one who bestows the vision of his own teaching upon the path to nirvāṇa, and who brings about the remainder [of beings] free from fear of bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and the like. || 14 ||
Homage to the one who is the parasol for the world, for those dwelling in the three realms;
to the one who effects liberation for all those freed from every affliction and disease. || 1 ||
"Nanda, O Nanda, lord of serpents, you who are adorned with the mountain of wisdom;
for the sake of beholding the beautiful form of the glorious Lord of the Unfailing Noose."
To the one who has attained all the qualities of mantra, who possesses true virtues, the great yakṣa Vajrapāṇi, whose hand holds the thunderbolt—[homage] to him. (175) 17.
To the one who assumes a terrifying form for the sake of the wicked beings in the three worlds, who is surrounded by spirits, ghosts, *kumbhāṇḍas*, *rākṣasas*, *yakṣas*, and other such [beings]. 18.
Homage to the one who has uprooted the thicket of afflictions, whose intellect is profound, whose wisdom is awakened, who has become all-knowing, and who has overcome all defilements.
On this earth, for one who has ascended the path of liberation through the practice of supreme dharma, there is no obstruction from unrighteousness nor any anxiety. || 20 ||
Having attained perfect enlightenment, he has purified his own mind and established others on the true path;
he is the one who brings about the complete liberation of beings from the afflictions of miserable rebirths such as the preta realm.
Homage to the one who possesses concentration numbering as many as the atoms of dust; homage always to Maitreya, the Lord of the World, the Bodhisattva. 22.
I bow to the Great Being who bestows the perfection of the qualities of the True Dharma; I always go for refuge to the Teacher of radiant splendor. (23)
O Lord of the World, be gracious to me who has committed this offense;
forgive what was done by me so that it may be as it was before.
Thus ends the *Japamālā* of the glorious Āryāvalokiteśvara.
Oṃ, homage to the Lord of the World!
I bow here to the Blessed One, who is renowned in the scriptures and in the world;
to the Great Lord who bears the lotus, and who bestows supreme joy upon Prahlāda.

Salutation to the one seated in the lotus posture, who is surrounded by the splendor of the lotus, who is perfectly auspicious, who holds a lotus in his hand, and who always bestows consolation upon the world. (2)
To the one who moves upon the earth, whose three eyes are perfectly pure, who wears a crown of jewels of the Victors, and who is adorned with the wish-fulfilling gem. || 3 ||
Thus ends the hymn composed by Maheśvara.
I bow here to the Blessed One, who shines as the Lord when the scriptures are contemplated;
to Maheśa, the sustainer of the world, the giver of life, the Great-Souled One. (1)
Homage to Pṛthivīvarana, to Trāyaṃ, to Śubhapadmadhara, to Padmaśrīpariṣṭata, and to Sūcetanakara. || 2 ||

Then indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, applying himself with even greater intensity to these successions of world-systems—incalculable and beyond expression—as well as to the supreme atoms of Buddha-fields throughout the expansion of kalpas, both auspicious and inauspicious, made this vow by means of verses: 1. [Verse follows]
As many as there are lions among men throughout all the worlds and the three realms, they have all gone to the state of Narasiṃha.
I fulfill all those aspirations with a serene body, speech, and mind. || 2 ||
With prostrations as numerous as the dust motes of the earth, I pay homage to all the Victors;
with a mind directed toward the presence of all the Victors, by the power of the *Bhadracarī* vow. (3)

Upon every single atom, I resolve with faith that there are immeasurable Buddhas and sons of the Buddhas seated in the midst of lotuses; in this way, I conceive the entire realm of phenomena to be completely filled with Victors. (4)
Within them, there are oceans of inexhaustible colors and oceans of all kinds of passion, expressed through their various sounds.
I shall praise all those Sugatas, proclaiming the virtues of all the Victors. (5)
With the finest flowers and the finest garlands, with excellent incense and supreme parasols, with the best lamps and the finest cloths, I perform worship to the Victors. (6)

With the finest garments and the finest perfumes, with powders and cloths as vast as Mount Meru, and with all the most distinguished and supreme incenses, I perform worship to those who have subdued their senses. (178) 7.
I resolve upon all those sublime and unsurpassed offerings for all the Victors;
through the power of my resolve in the *Bhadracaryā*, I pay homage to and worship all the Victors. (8)
Whatever sin has been committed by me under the influence of passion, hatred, or delusion, through body, speech, or mind—even if it be slight—I confess all of it here and now. 9.

Whatever merit exists in the ten directions belonging to those in training, those beyond training, the Pratyekabuddhas, the sons of the Buddhas, and all the Victors—I rejoice in all of that, without exception. (10)

And those lamps of the world in the ten directions who have awakened to enlightenment and attained non-attachment—to all of them, O Śakra, I exhort you to turn the wheel of the Dharma as has been taught by the Tathāgatas. (11)
And those who desire to teach the state of nirvāṇa, may they remain as long as I have not yet attained omniscience;
for the sake of the happiness of all the world, may they serve as causes for the welfare of beings for kalpas as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field. 12.

Whatever merit has been accumulated by me through prostration, worship, teaching, protection, rejoicing, requesting [the Buddhas to teach], and entreating [them to remain], may all of it be dedicated unerringly toward supreme enlightenment. 13.

(179) May the Buddhas of the past be honored; may those who currently dwell in the worlds of the ten directions, and those who will appear in the future, swiftly fulfill their aspirations and awaken to enlightenment. 14.
May all the fields whatsoever that exist in the ten directions become pure and sublime.
May these [offerings] be fully perfected by the sons of the Buddha who have gone to the king of Bodhi trees for alms. || 15 ||
May whatever sentient beings there are in the ten directions become happy and free from disease; and may all the world’s righteous purposes be fulfilled, and their hopes be realized. (16)
While practicing the conduct of awakening, may I remember my births in all states of existence; in every birth and every rebirth, may I go forth into homelessness. 17.
Training myself in the teachings of all the Victors and fulfilling the conduct of excellence, may I always practice the stainless and pure conduct of ethical discipline, unbroken and flawless. 18.

Through the sounds of the gods, and even the sounds of non-humans, through the sounds of yakṣas, kumbhāṇḍas, and humans—whatever sounds exist in the world, he perceives them all and teaches the Dharma with a beautiful voice. (19)
Those who are indeed devoted to the perfections shall never be bound; and whatever obscuring dharmas there may be, they shall be completely extinguished without remainder. (20)

May I move through the worlds that have fallen under the power of Māra and the cruel deeds of karma with unhindered gait; like a lotus unsullied by mud, or like the sun and moon in the sky, may I remain unattached. May I pacify the sufferings of the lower realms and establish all beings in the Dharma;
may I act for the welfare of the entire world, like the wind blowing in every direction. (21)
Following after the conduct of all beings, fulfilling the conduct of awakening, and spreading abroad the auspicious conduct, may I practice throughout all future eons. (22)

Those who have requested me, the Sugata, may they all come together in this very existence; whether by moment, by hour, by thought, or by word, may they share a single aspiration and a single course of conduct. (23)

And those friends and companions who desire my welfare, and those who seek to promote the *Bhadracaryā*, may they always be my teachers; with devotion, I shall never cease to honor them throughout all births. (181) || 24 ||

May I always behold the Victors face-to-face, as well as the Buddhas’ sons and the Lords who have entered parinirvāṇa; and may I see all those noble ones who perform worship to them, throughout all future eons. (25)
The Conquerors who uphold the True Dharma illuminate the supreme enlightenment.
And purifying Bhadraṃvarī, he shall practice throughout all future eons. || 26 ||
Transmigrating through all realms of existence, he has attained inexhaustible merit and wisdom;
with insight, skillful means, meditative concentration, and liberation, he is an inexhaustible treasury of all virtues. (27)

Even if one were to protect as many atoms as there are grains of dust on a single atom of a king’s realm with unwavering action, while dwelling in the midst of the ocean after having renounced the Buddhas and the sons of the Buddhas, yet still seeking the supreme conduct of awakening—(this would not equal even a fraction of the merit of the former). || 28 ||

Thus, throughout all directions without exception, within the realms of ignorant beings, [I shall] constantly utter the ocean of Buddhas, the oceans of royal lineages, the oceans of names, the oceans of *kalpas* as beautiful as the color of gold, and the purity of the vocal range of all Victors within the oceans of sounds of the Lord’s passion, according to the inclinations and languages of the entire world— the eloquence of the Buddha. (182)

Through the power of the Buddha, may I enter into the turning of the methods of the speech and sounds of the three times, which proclaim the voices of all the Victors throughout the three periods of time. 31.
Without a moment's delay, may I enter all future eons; and those three eons that are being proclaimed, may I practice throughout them for tens of millions of *koṭis* of years.
Having perceived in a single instant those lions among men who have appeared throughout the three times,
he always offers prostrations to them by means of the power of liberation that is like an illusion.
Just as the thunderbolt with its golden tip destroys the dwellings of the Asuras in the three worlds,
so too does the arm of the Victors destroy the enemies of the world in all directions without exception.

Those very future lamps of the world, having awakened to them, shall set in motion the wheel [of Dharma]; and those who are established in vision and peace—unto them he has come to pay his respects. (35)
By the power of his resolve, he is all-pervading; by his non-abiding, he is all-facing.
By the power of his conduct, he possesses universal virtues; by the shelter of his loving-kindness, he has gone everywhere. (36)
By the power of merit, by all-pervading auspiciousness, and by the power of unattached compassion;
through the power of wisdom, skillful means, and meditative concentration, he fully realizes the power of awakening. || 37 ||
Purifying the power of karma, crushing the power of the afflictions, and beholding the power of Māra—O you whose strength is the entire noble conduct of Samantabhadra! || 38 ||
Purifying the oceans of fields, liberating the oceans of sentient beings, discerning the ocean of Dharma, and plunging into the ocean of primordial wisdom. || 39 ||
Purifying oceans of conduct, fulfilling oceans of vows, and honoring oceans of Buddhas, may I practice for oceans of eons without weariness. (40)
Having fulfilled all those special vows and practices for enlightenment of the Victors who have gone by the path in the past, may I awaken to that enlightenment which is the Good Conduct. 41.
I dedicate all this merit to him whose name is Samantabhadra, the eldest son of all the Victors, so that his conduct may become equal to mine. 42.
Through the purification of body, speech, and mind, one should practice according to the rules; thus, there is the purification of the three spheres.
O wise ones, understand it to be just as it is named.
According to my own opinion. || 43 ||
This is the supreme vow of Mañjuśrī, which is auspicious and entirely pure.
Indeed, may he fulfill all these [vows] without exception, remaining untiring throughout all future eons. (44)
May there be victory over the assault of Māra.
Do not consider my virtues to be immeasurable; having set out upon the path of the immeasurable, you yourself shall know all their miraculous transformations. 45.
As long as you remain in the sky without remainder until your final nirvana, and as long as your karma remains, may my prayer endure for that same duration. 46.

And whatever infinite realms of light adorned with jewels exist in the ten directions belonging to the Victors—excellent with divine and human happiness—one might give them away for as many eons as there are atoms in a constellation. (47)

And whoever, having heard this King of Transferences, develops faith in it with a virtuous mind, and aspiring to the conduct of awakening, becomes disciplined—may they possess such merit as this. (48)
By avoiding them, the states of woe are avoided; by avoiding them, bad friends are avoided.
Behold Amitābha, who quickly beholds him; behold the ocean of his conduct and his vows. (49)
O you who live with greed as your companion, welcome to you in this birth!
For just as Samantabhadra is, so too are those who have honored him. || 50 ||

One who has committed evil deeds and lacks immediate fruits [of merit], yet has acted under the power of ignorance—by reciting this *Bhadracarī*, such a person quickly exhausts that [evil] entirely. (51)
He is endowed with a form equal to that of the Knower, and likewise possessed of a nature that has transcended all worldly existence.
Unassailable by the hosts of heretical paths, he shall be honored throughout the entire triple world. || 52 ||
He quickly goes to the king of Bodhi trees and, having gone there, sits down for the welfare of sentient beings.
With his awakening, he shall proclaim enlightenment; he will subdue all the wicked ones along with their armies. 53.
Whoever has upheld, recited, or taught this sublime *Samantabhadra-praṇidhāna*,
the Buddha knows that their ripening of karma will be exceptionally distinguished among the people of the world. (54)
Whatever merit Mañjuśrī possesses, as well as that of Samantabhadra, and whatever else exists—I, Mañjuśrī, while passing away, dedicate all this merit toward them. 55.

(186) Whatever supreme transformation of merit has been described by the Victors who have gone to the three times, may I, through all that merit, attain the state of a Buddha, the most excellent of beings.
At the time of death, having turned away from all pride and egoistic conceit,
one should face Amitābha directly and behold that very Sukhāvatī realm.
May all those aspirations directed toward that [enlightenment] be fully realized in every existence;
may I completely fulfill them all,
and act for the benefit of sentient beings throughout the world.
There, in that most excellent and beautiful city of Anūlaśobhana, he was born;
and there he obtained the grammatical treatise in the presence of the Jina Amitābha.

He delights in the grammatical exposition; having established many hundreds of millions of emanations within it, he would perform the welfare of sentient beings even in the ten directions by means of his buddha-power.
Having recited the *Bhadracarīpraṇidhāna*, whatever merit has been accumulated by me,
may all that be dedicated in a single instant toward the auspicious aspiration for the welfare of the world.
May Bhadravārī, having transformed the merit acquired by me— which is exceedingly distinguished—
cause this world, submerged in the flood of calamities, to go to the supreme city of Amitābha.
The Noble Great Vow of Bhadracarī, the King of Jewels, is completed.
Oṃ, homage to the Protector of the World!
Oṃ, homage to the glorious Noble Avalokiteśvara.
To the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, the Greatly Compassionate One.

Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying on Mount Āryāvalokita, on the peak of Mount Pāṭala, which was strewn with thousands of jewel-trees and illuminated by the luster of Jāmbūnada gold.
He dwelt in a region of the earth consisting of celestial palaces made of various jewels.

There, the Blessed One— honored, revered, esteemed, worshiped, venerated, and respected by many hundreds of thousands of millions of *asuras*, *nāgas*, *yakṣas*, gods, *garuḍas*, *kinnaras*, *mahoragas*, and *tuṣitas*— sat surrounded by them and taught the Dharma.

He proclaimed the Dharma that is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end; which is meaningful and well-expressed, unique, complete, perfectly pure, and fully purified in its practice.

Then indeed the Vṛndida gods praised the noble Avalokiteśvara: "O Blessed One, you have done what was to be done; you have accomplished your task; you have laid down the burden; you have attained your own goal; the fetters of existence are destroyed; your mind is perfectly liberated through right knowledge;

you are well-liberated in conduct; you are a thoroughbred, a great elephant; you have attained supreme mastery over all states of mind; you have reached the highest perfection; you are complete in the equipment of merit and wisdom; you have crossed the wilderness of existence; you strive for the benefit of others; your heart is bound with great compassion."

He who treats all beings as his own supreme children, the bestower of happiness, whose fame is spread by his great affection for his sons, and who brings across the infinite multitude of sentient beings.
The son of the Sugata, who has made a vow to perform what is wholesome, is the sole kinsman of the three worlds.

Free from illness, free from hatred, free from delusion, and having cast off the three types of death; having reached the further shore of the triple world and attained the six supernormal powers; with limbs rounded like those of a Naga; bearing the thirty-two marks of a Great Man; his body adorned with the eighty minor characteristics; possessing a golden complexion and a form as pure and bright as a white parasol;
with hair like that of a Naga.

Wearing beautiful matted locks, with a crown of matted hair rising upward, his radiance—like immeasurable rays of light—blazes through the sky; he possesses the splendor of refined gold and is endowed with vast majesty. He has the sun as his turban, his upper body is adorned with blazing jewels and sacrificial threads, he is established in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), and he has fulfilled the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*).

He whose virtue is unbroken and whose conduct is flawless; who has the onset of a lion’s prowess and the stride of a lion; whose roar is deep and who possesses the lion’s roar and the universal roar; whose limbs are delicate and graceful; whose gait is like that of a bull;

who has a beautiful navel that spirals to the right; whose navel is deep; whose forehead is adorned with a crescent moon; whose lips are red as the *viṣṭira* fruit; whose arms are long; whose shoulders are closely set; whose nose is prominent; and whose neck is shaped like a conch shell.

He has long arms and slender fingers; he resembles a sword, a treasure, a necklace, and a lotus; his limbs are lean yet pure; his voice is deep and resonant, reaching the heart and inspiring joy; he is lovely, beautiful to behold, and pleasing to see. He possesses the delightful color of Jāmbūnada gold; he is adorned with lotuses upon his eyes;

he is born from a lotus, arisen from a lotus, seated upon a lotus, having a lotus-like face, and holding a lotus in his hand. He holds a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) in his hand, wears a black antelope skin, and carries a triple staff, a rosary of beads, a lotus, and a sacred thread. He is the primordial one.

The monk Amṛtavarṣa is like a wish-fulfilling gem, like a beautiful kalpavṛkṣa tree; he is the bestower of wealth upon all sentient beings, the pacifier of all diseases, the bringer of joy, the supreme refuge for all sentient beings, and the emanation-body of the Buddha. He wears the garb of a Sugata, bears the relics of a Sugata, and has brought all sentient beings in every single atom of the world-system to the end of saṃsāra. He has accomplished merit, fulfilled his purpose, completed what was to be done, perfected his virtue, and reached firm resolve; he is one whose vigor is blazing.

He has transcended saṃsāra; he is consecrated with the jewel of the true Dharma; his feet follow Tārā; he is one who recognizes kindness through his frown; he is victorious, possessed of right conduct, and possessed of mindfulness; he possesses great valor, virtue, the power of loving-kindness, ethical discipline, compassion, and tranquility.

They were mindful, fortunate, wealthy, givers of wealth, dispellers of doubts, expounders of the Dharma, and teachers of the world. Their faces possessed full moon-like countenances; their dwellings were adorned with all kinds of jewels; they were of beautiful form and appearance. With a splendor exceeding a thousand suns, they shone with radiant bodies like Indra, the lord of the gods, at the beginning of the aeon. (191) Thus it is said.

The Blessed One, with the eye of wisdom, has seen that the world is both peaceful and unpeaceful; yet, due to the obscuration of conceptualization, it does not arise as it truly is, appearing instead as both existent and non-existent.
How can that which is not produced from itself nor from another be born?
For it is held that a cause is neither identical to its effect nor different from it.
In this interval, there is neither non-existence nor existence, nor is there anything other than these two.
If [the self and the world] were one, the destruction of existence would follow;
if they were separate, the non-destruction of existence would follow.
First, when a cause has perished, the arising of an effect is not tenable;
nor, according to your own doctrine, is the arising of an effect admitted by means of a non-perished self-nature.
The Buddha is born from the seed-syllable of the Buddha, arising from the family.
The arising of that which is like an illusion is taught as being the very nature of all things.
Therefore, having thus conceptualized this world, it arises perfectly.
When fully understood, it becomes equanimity, characterized by non-arising and non-affliction;
this is declared as the constant mindfulness and recollection of those who know reality, the pinnacle of the sky.
The Lord of those who know reality has declared that memory is like a dream;
it destroys what was done by oneself and brings about the great fruit of what was done by another.
What suffering will he cause you? One should abandon that which you have described;
for that which is dependent origination is always emptiness itself.
"An independent entity does not exist"—this is the eighth lion's roar here.
For the purpose of removing all conceptual constructions, emptiness was taught as the state of death.
Even in that [state], you have instilled a grasp of this speech;
O Māyāvatī, may those born of the lotus lead you to the state of Śivakāsinī.
O Protector, you have revealed that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature; nothing whatsoever has been added by you, nor has anything thought out been obstructed.
As it was before, so it is after; thus have you awakened.
The noble dharma has been sprinkled [upon you]; here, there is not even a slight cultivation [of signs]. For consciousness arises here in no way whatsoever through signs.
For consciousness here cannot possibly become signless in any way;
and [the Buddha] declared that there is no liberation without resorting to the signless. Therefore, the Mahāyāna was taught by you as a skillful means for that purpose.
Having heard this merit which I have spoken, and having understood that you are a vessel for liberation,

Vajrapāṇi is at the eastern gate; Lokanātha is at the western gate;
Mañjuśrīkumāra is at the northern gate.
In the northeastern corner are all the planets;
in the southeastern corner are all the lunar mansions.
In the southwest corner, all calamities [are pacified].
In the northwestern corner is the Great Goddess Bhaṭṭārikā.
White, blue, and red in her three faces, each face possessing two eyes, she has six arms; with two hands she displays the *vyākhyāna* (teaching) mudrā;
she holds a vajra in her right hands and a lotus in her left hands.
Wearing a jewel crown, seated upon a diamond throne, she has entered [the mandala] and is comfortably seated on a moon-disc seat.
With bodies sixteen years of age and adorned with all ornaments,
they [are placed] at the eastern gate of the mandala, outside [the enclosure], for Dhṛtarāṣṭra, with curd-rice as their offering.
On the right, there is a vessel of curd-rice belonging to Dīrgha.
In the west, [the offering] for Virapākṣa is milk-rice; in the north, for Kubera, it is curd-rice;
and for Sindhulasa, it is equal [to that].
Worship with flowers and other offerings should be performed according to the sequence of the different colors.
A lamp should be offered for each [deity]. Having filled a conch with ghee and honey and having cast five jewels into it, the *arghya* offering should be presented.
One should place [the offering] into the mouths of all with a goad.
Such are the colors, arm postures, hand gestures, and emblems that they possess.
Oṃ, homage to all Tathāgatas, who completely fulfill all aspirations; in every way, to devotion, svāhā!
The mantra of the Three Jewels.

The mantras of the seven, the seven, and the eight [planets] were thus worshipped by Vajrapāṇi; the heart-mantras of the nine planets became perfected.
Having prepared a fragrant mandala according to the specific distinctions of the sequence of the yakṣas, one should perform the worship in the center of a mandala measuring ten finger-breadths.

Having offered the *arghya* with a vessel made of copper, clay, silver, or other materials, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times; thereafter, while holding a vajra in hand, the mantra-words of the *Grahamātṛkā-nāma-dhāraṇī* should be uttered seven times.
Then all those planets, beginning with Āditya, will provide protection, a shield, and concealment.
I shall liberate everyone from the grasp of poverty;
may those whose life-span has expired regain their life.

For those who have not met with untimely death, they shall not die prematurely.
O Vajrapāṇi, whoever indeed shall worship [this] in the midst of the maṇḍala of the planets and recite it day after day, [he shall obtain the fruits].
Then all the *grahas* will completely fulfill every single hope of that Dharma-reciter.
Even from that family, those who are impoverished will lie down [to die].
Then indeed, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, again spoke this *dhāraṇī* called the *Mātṛkāvigraha*.

Oṃ! To the Buddha, to the Vajra, to the Lotus, to the Arrow, spread forth, spread forth! Remember, remember! Play, play! Cause to play, cause to play! Kill, kill! Slay, slay! Crush, crush! Fulfill the purpose of myself and my retinue and of all sentient beings! Drive away, drive away! All sins, for me and my retinue, be pacified, be pacified! Be tamed, be tamed!

2 Dāpaya 2! Quickly reveal yourself, O Blessed One! Protect us and all sentient beings; dispel the afflictions caused by all planetary spirits (*graha*) and constellations (*nakṣatra*). In existence after existence, O Fierce One, O Most Fierce One, O Heat, O Burning Heat! Fulfill [our desires], O Blessed One!

O Vajrapāṇi, this dhāraṇī named Gṛhamātṛkā should be recited during the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, beginning on the seventh day and continuing until the fourteenth, when one has fasted; then, on the full moon day at the great hour of midnight, having performed the preliminary rites, it should be recited. For one who does so, there will be no fear of death for ninety-nine years; nor will there be the falling of meteors, the affliction of planets, or any fear.
With each act of patience, he will become one who remembers his former births.
Then all those planetary spirits (grahas) replied, "Very well," and having bowed down, they said, "May we not be harmed."
Thus spoke the Blessed One, and the venerable Śāriputra, that entire assembly, along with the gods, humans, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken.
Thus ends the noble *Gṛhamātṛkā-nāma-dhāraṇī*.
Oṃ, homage to Rāhu!

Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling in the great city of Aḍakavatī on a lion throne, which was empowered by the empowerment of Laṅkā and the Great Vajra-samaya, surrounded by many gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, apasmāras, Āditya, Soma, Agni, Budha, Bṛhaspati, Śukra, Śaniścara, Rāhu, Ketu, and the twenty-eight lunar mansions and others who were paying him honor.
Together with many hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Rāma-maitreya,
surrounded and honored by hundreds of thousands of such great Bodhisattvas, was teaching the Dharma.

Rahu, blazing with splendor and terrifying, having assumed the form of a sage, approached the sky; he was devoid of light, his body dark blue like a cloud, his face distorted, his eyes like jewels, and his form terrifying with a gaping mouth, appearing like a dark mountain peak.
The fierce Rāhu, having ascended the lion throne, seized the sun and moon with his terrible and hideous form.
His body is composed of the perishable, the imperishable, and the eternal; he is endowed with the primordial body, white as a conch shell, and adorned with auspicious black marks.
To Rāhu, son of Siṃha, lover of nectar, whose deity is Kuśeśvara.
To the one who wears black garments, who is black, whose fragrance is black, and who is adorned with black sacrificial threads.

O Lord, please descend for the benefit of me, the sacrificer, together with the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, and the hosts of yakṣas. Having entered here into the midst of the sacrificial fire, may you, the bringer of peace, accomplish the purpose of Rāhu, for whom this act of propitiation is performed. Thus spoke Śrī Vajrapāṇi.
O Blessed One, [this was spoken] by Rāhanya Siṃhasuta, Amṛtapriya, and Kurīseśvara Devata.
May the lifespan of all sentient beings be protected from diseases such as those caused by *nāgas* and other spirits.
They caused sentient beings to dwell [in happiness].
They were afflicted by calamities.
Some were robbed of their wealth.
They were taking away the life-breath of some.
In this way, they were driven away, causing distress to all sentient beings.
At that time, O Blessed One, all sentient beings became devoted to this Dharma discourse, the Essence of the Dharma.

Oṃ! To Rāhava, to the Sun and the Thousand Moons, to the one with a sword and shield, to the one whose hair is tied upward on the crown of the head, to the one with a distorted face set in a frown, to the one who destroys all fears!
Homage, homage to the one who pacifies previous diseases; homage to the deity Rādbhū.

May all diseases arising from the elements, from the spirits, from wind, from bile, from phlegm, or from their combination, as well as those caused by the consumption of poison, be pacified; may all obstacles be stilled for Rāhu, who drinks the nectar.
The venerable Vājapāṇi said this: "He who goes, rejoicing."
The Noble Dhāraṇī for the Pacification of Seizures by Non-human Beings and the Removal of Calamities is hereby completed.
Oṃ, homage to the noble Āryakatava.

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Blessed One was dwelling in Aṅkacaityā together with gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, Apasmāra, Āditya, Soma, Aṅgāra, Budha, Bṛhaspati, Śukra, Śanaiścara, Rāhu, Ketu, and the twenty-eight constellations (*nakṣatra*), as well as many bodhisattvas, teaching the Dharma.
Then Vajrahā approached the Blessed One and said this to him: "O Blessed One, fierce beings have made a cave; they are violent and cruel, and they are destroying living beings with firebrands."
In some cases it causes affliction; in others, it carries away life.
In this way, he bestowed the gift of Dharma that removes all calamities for all sentient beings.
The Blessed One said:
"Excellent, excellent, Vajrapāṇi! Listen well and attend closely; I shall speak. Now, he taught the Ketugraha [constellation]."
To the son of Kāśyapa, who had taken up the single mendicant’s bowl, Khaṅga was the family deity.

O you who are clothed in smoke, whose flowers are smoke, whose incense and lamps are smoke, whose sacrifice is smoke; O Purifier! For the sake of pleasing [the deity], for the one dwelling in smoke, for the one who has ascended, for the God accompanied by Dānavas, Kumbhāṇḍas, and Ḍākinīs—O Blessed One, for the benefit of all beings, enter this house, the center of the maṇḍala; may they desire joy, grant prosperity, and perform nourishment for the Blessed One. You whose various and diverse minds adorn the earth, you who hold a shield and a noose in your hands, you who possess the knowledge of the leather-noose, you who have renewed the face, you who hold the name of the distracted one as a blessing.

To the one whose body possesses the splendor of ten million *yūketu* stars, who is like smoke, non-smoke, well-smoking, incomparable, smokeless, and of the color of the ocean; who is adorned with the crest of a peacock feather; who is the sole refuge for those seeking protection; who holds a sword in his hand; who is the deity of the Khadga lineage;
and who has conquered Māra—may there be the attainment of health and prosperity.
Vajrapāṇi said:
Oṃ, homage to the one whose banner is unbearable to behold, resembling the fire of universal destruction.
For the sake of the welfare of the worlds, may he [be] free from disease and free from all specific ailments.
And the planets, O Blessed One, were fierce, having the forms of Rudra, cruel and most cruel; they obstructed the path and created obstacles for him.
Some were snatching away vitality, some were carrying off possessions, and some were taking away their very lives.

In this very way, they caused all sentient beings to be carried away by the flood of calamities.
Furthermore, for all calamities of this kind and of the twelve [types], there is no other protection.

Oṃ buddha 2, śuddha 2, vajra 2, padme 2, sara 2, prasara 2, sāra 2, krīḍya 2! Accomplish all my activities! Sever [all obstacles]! Destroy all malevolent ones! Be peaceful! Grant [blessings]! Quickly show [yourself]! O Māra-protector, protect me and all sentient beings from the fear and affliction of all planets and constellations! Svāhā!

O Blessed One, O Great Illusion! Purify all views; O Caṇḍacaṇḍinī, for all beings! *Turu* 2, *sūma* 2, *mūñca* 2! Summon, summon! O fierce one, O fierce one, O goddess of speech! O Blessed One, fulfill the heart’s desire of all sentient beings! By the power of the pledge presided over by all the Tathāgatas, *svāhā*!
Thus spoke the Blessed One, and the Great Vajrapāṇi rejoiced exceedingly.
The Noble Dhāraṇī for the Pacification of Planetary Influences is hereby completed.
Oṃ, to Nako Viprāntaka!

O Great Hero who brings an end to the destruction of the wise, O Destroyer of the obstacles of the three worlds! You are adorned with a crown of matted hair as white as Mount Sumeru, topped by five skulls; you are resplendent with a complexion like the color of a dark cloud. Standing upon the back of an elephant, your forehead shines with a third eye that blazes like the sun.
Adorned with serpent-earrings and necklaces of jewels, you are manifested from the primordial light, endowed with all protective powers.
This Lord bears six arms; He holds a sword, a shield, and a supreme lotus; He is wide awake in great passion. In His left hands, He holds a skull-staff, a severed head, and a garland of human limbs;
He holds an elephant-hide. His pair of feet rest upon the shoulders of an enemy, and He is beautifully adorned with an elephant-hide and a tiger-skin draped over His waist.

Adorned with necklaces, half-necklaces, bracelets, and elephant-hide, he who brings about the eight aims of the southern direction, who is the remover of the suffering of all sentient beings, and who is devoted to the teacher of song—homage to him!

I bow to the King of Mūlakroḍa, who possesses the grace of the six-faced one (Kārttikeya), who is the nectar of the Vedas, who is the void of the ten directions, who nourishes the darbha grass, who is auspiciously dark, who is the essence of the lotus, and who is borne by the host of ten-faced ones (Rāvaṇa).
Thus ends the Daśakroḍadhāraṇī.

Therefore, there is no difference.

All diseases are destroyed; may there be well-being for me and for all sentient beings, and may all illness, calamities, and misfortunes be pacified. Svāhā!

O sustainer of existence!

in Kāti-caraṇa; in Sālegri-śānti-svabhūmu; for me and for all sentient beings, in the southern direction, svāhā!

May these flowers and incense accept my spoken offering,
through your hundredfold heroisms, your sovereign power, and your strength.
All diseases are destroyed; may there be well-being for me and for all sentient beings from all fears, calamities, and misfortunes. Svāhā!

Salutations to you, O heroic Puruṣa; salutations to you, O Puruṣa who is the Supreme Light. We bow to the one whose hand holds the wheel of Dharma; salutations to you who possess the vigor of righteousness.

you who have rescued the brown-haired one from the harshness of the forest.

accept this flower and incense; may there be prosperity for me.
By their vigor, splendor, sovereignty, and power, may all diseases be destroyed for myself and for all sentient beings, and [may there be freedom] from all fears, calamities, and afflictions; svāhā!

O wielder of the thunderbolt;

To myself, to both, to all sentient beings, and to the cardinal and intermediate directions, svāhā!
Vaiśravaṇa, Śakra, the World-Protectors,

accepting this flower and incense, may you remain free from anger and harm.
By means of their vigor, majesty, splendor, and the Śaryyāṇavat mountain.

Salutations to you, O Puruṣottama; salutations to you, O Supreme Puruṣa; salutations to Umāpati, the Lord of Justice (Dharmarāja); salutations to you, the Unborn One.
