Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke this verse:
In this world, which is filled with the most excellent fragrances, there dwell in the heavens those who are like jewels;
they abide there through the power of the Tathāgata, the God of Gods, the Supreme among Men, who stands in perfect equanimity.
Therefore, this jewel-like word has been well-spoken; by this, may there be well-being for us today.

Cessation is dispassion; the Deathless is the unconditioned. Having realized the well-taught, supreme, and auspicious Dharma—the peaceful, unconditioned, and deathless—by means of this truth, may there be well-being here for all beings.
This is the most excellent of jewels. By this truth, may there be well-being here.
This desired practice, which brings about the vehicle of yoga, has been duly proclaimed by the Teacher on the noble seat;
there is no concentration equal to this, which is like a diamond and reveals the non-dual path.
Therefore, by this truth that this excellent jewel is sublime, may there be well-being here and in the hereafter.
The eight great purifying qualities are well-known; these four are declared to be worthy of offerings.
They were sung by the Sugata, the Great Sage, who is perfectly full of compassion.
A gift given here yields great fruit, just as seeds sown in a good field do.
By the truth of this sublime and excellent Jewel of the Saṅgha, may there be well-being here and in that [other] place.
Those who approach the teaching of Gautama with a clear mind and resolute effort—
having reached it— they attain the deathless state, having dispelled the darkness of doubt and attained cessation.
This sublime and excellent jewel of the Saṅgha—by this, may there be well-being here in this world!
Through the simultaneous application [of the path], there is the vision of the truths; therein, the three afflictions are abandoned all at once:
the view of a self-identity, doubt, and the adherence to rites and rituals, as well as the adherence to [wrong] views.
This supreme gift has been offered here to the Jewel of the Saṅgha by this person.

One should never commit the threefold evil— whether by body, speech, or mind— even for the sake of wealth; nor should one conceal it, for that which is done impulsively is not seen by those who possess innate wisdom.
This is the sublime Jewel of the Sangha; by this truth, may there be well-being here and now.
Just as the earth is firmly established upon the moon-pillar and is unshaken by the winds from the four directions,
so too do those who behold the supreme Noble Path shine like lotuses within the Saṅgha.
This is the sublime and excellent Jewel of the Saṅgha; by this truth, may there be well-being here and now.
Those who do not practice the Noble Truths taught by profound wisdom, and who do not apply their minds to the gift of the [Buddhist] scriptures, do not attain the unsurpassed, supreme state.
This is the sublime and excellent Jewel of the Saṅgha; by this truth, may there be well-being here.

Just as the eight limbs of the army, when destroyed by the power of the wind, no longer count as such; even so, the sons of the Buddha, having abandoned the fetters, go to the state beyond perception. This is the sublime and excellent Jewel of the Saṅgha; through this, may there be well-being here.

May all beings in this world and beyond, whether high or low, be happy; may they pay homage here to the Teacher, the supreme Buddha, the god among men, the best of bipeds, and may there be well-being for them.
May all those sentient beings, both moving and stationary, who have been our mothers, fathers, brothers, sisters, and so forth, become happy;
and may there be well-being here through the homage paid to the Dharma, which is peaceful, supreme, and honored by gods and men.
May all beings—whether moving or stationary, whether born from wombs or otherwise—be happy.
O gods and men, pay homage here to the assembly, the foremost among congregations; may there be well-being for us in this world.

May it be auspicious! This concludes the Noble *Parimitā* Dhāraṇī Mahāyāna Sūtra, as recited by the venerable Śrī Dhīrja at Vāhālamūla, which was heard by the world of Gandharvas and rejoiced in as the word of the Blessed One. Thus ends the summary.
Oṃ, homage to the glorious Śrī Lokanātha!
Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling on Mount Potalaka.

The Noble Avalokiteśvara was in his abode, which was adorned with many *śāla* trees, mango groves, and various jewel-trees; there, together with a great community of monks consisting of eighteen thousand monks and nine hundred thousand *koṭi-niyuta-śata-sahasra* bodhisattvas,

and surrounded and honored by many hundreds of thousands of *koṭi-niyuta-śata-sahasra* sons of gods from the Śuddhāvāsa realm, he taught the Dharma, addressing the sons of gods such as Īśvara, Maheśvara, and Brahmakāyika.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, rising from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and,
bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, spoke these words to the Blessed One with a smiling face.

“Blessed One, today I possess the King of Nooses, the Heart of the Nāga, which I previously received from the presence of the Tathāgata Lokendra-rāja in the world-system Vilokitā during a single eon. By means of this, Blessed One, hundreds of thousands of gods, led by the sons of the gods of the Pure Abodes, have been inspired toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.”
With a mind free from delusion, he dwells in a hundred thousand samādhis, headed by the Array of Knowledge.

And in whatever place on earth, O Blessed One, this *Udayapāśahṛdaya* might fall, it should be known that in that region twelve hundred thousand sons of gods, headed by Īśvara, Maheśvara, and Brahmakāyika, will provide protection, shelter, and defense; and that place on earth, O Blessed One, will become like a sanctuary.
Where the tenth mudrā-pāśa shall move within the heart,
there will be beings who have been purified by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas.
Those who shall dry up this heart-entrapping snare for the sake of joy; |||
O Blessed One, whoever might be a doer of evil deeds, one who practices all unwholesome dharmas, and a speaker of falsehoods— (535)— [may they be purified].
One who rejects the true Dharma.
One who is intent on non-retrogression, who has transcended all fetters, and who is a noble disciple of the Bodhisattvas and Buddhas—should he feel remorse, let him go, O Noble One, to the forest.
For it is there that his karma may be purified; it does not become purified in this very birth, nor does it reach its end or pass away here.
It is not through a single-day fever, nor a three-day fever, nor a four-day fever, nor even through a five-day fever that it is so.

Whether suffering from pain in the sword-like [chest], or pain in the nose, or pain in the ears, or pain in the lips, or pain in the teeth, or pain in the head, or indeed pain in the heart, or pain in the abdomen, or pain in the sides, or pain in the back, or pain in the limbs and minor members, or pain in the *alasa* and *agrahaṇī*, or in diarrhea (*atisāra*).
